title: How big is a force? Invent a unit, then meet the newton
playtest: Checked at home in thought, step by step. The coin pull works on a wooden or laminate table with thin school notebooks: one notebook usually needs 5 to 10 five-rupee coins, and a stack of two needs about twice as many. If one notebook needs more than 12 coins, use thinner notebooks or a smoother table. If it slides with no coins, the cup is too heavy. A cushion under the cup stops coins rolling away. Counts vary by a coin or two between tries, which is why each test is done 3 times. The water version needs a medicine cup or jug with millilitre marks. A real forcemeter is needed only for the Go deeper parts.

summary.text: How many coins does it take to pull a notebook across a table? You and your cousin can both count carefully and still get different numbers. Both of you can be right. That puzzle is why the whole world agreed to share one unit of force, the newton. You will invent your own unit and meet the forcemeter. Then you will follow pulls from a molecule in your body to the Moon.
summary.art: A child holding a spring forcemeter with an apple hanging from its hook, the pointer on 1 N. Behind her is a ladder of pictures from a feather up to a rocket.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. Hold a 100 gram packet in one hand and a 1 kilogram packet of atta in the other. How many times harder does the big one pull? Now, how could you tell a friend in another city exactly how hard it pulls?
intro.text: Words like 'heavy' and 'light' don't travel well. Your 'heavy' may be your grandmother's 'light'. A shopkeeper selling rice, a builder hanging a bridge and a doctor testing your grip all need something better. They need a number that means the same thing to everyone. Where does such a number come from? Nature does not print numbers on things. You will start by making up your own unit of pull. Then you will find out what goes wrong when other people make up theirs.
intro.art: A child with eyes closed holding a small packet in one hand and a big atta packet in the other, a big question mark above.

outcomes: I can invent my own unit of pull, such as 'one coin', and use it to compare pulls.
I can explain why two careful people can get different numbers for one pull. I can say why we need one agreed unit.
I can say that forces are counted in newtons. One newton is about the pull of a small apple. I can explain that the newton is an agreement between people.
I can use a forcemeter properly. I check the zero, pull steadily, read the scale at eye level and write the unit.
I can explain how a forcemeter works: a spring stretches more when the pull is bigger.
I can make a guess with a reason and test it fairly. I can say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can explain that weight is a force, so the same bag would give a smaller number on the Moon.
I can say what a force does and what a push is underneath. I can name something scientists still do not know about forces.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces make things start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, turn or change shape.
terms.example: You pull a drawer open. You push a door shut.
terms.art: A hand pulling a drawer and a hand pushing a door, with arrows.

terms.meaning: How strong a push or a pull is. Scientists also call it the strength of the force.
terms.example: Lifting a pencil takes a small pull. Lifting a full bucket takes a big pull.
terms.art: A small arrow lifting a pencil and a long thick arrow lifting a bucket.

terms.meaning: To find how big something is by counting how many units it takes to match it.
terms.example: A pencil is 15 centimetres long, because 15 centimetre steps fit along it. A notebook's pull is 6 coins, because 6 coins in a cup start it sliding.
terms.art: A pencil lying beside a ruler, and a notebook pulled by a cup with six coins in it.

terms.meaning: One agreed amount that we count again and again. Centimetres are a unit of length. Newtons are a unit of force.
terms.example: In the coin-pull test, your unit was the pull of one coin. 'Six' meant six of those pulls.
terms.art: Three labels: 5 cm, 5 coins, 5 N, each on a matching object.

terms.meaning: The thing everyone agrees to check their unit against, so that everyone's unit is the same size.
terms.example: From 1889 to 2019, one metal cylinder near Paris was the standard kilogram. Every other kilogram was checked against it.
terms.art: A shiny metal cylinder under three glass bell jars, with a small label 'the kilogram'.

terms.meaning: The unit of force that scientists everywhere agreed to share. It is named after the scientist Isaac Newton. The short way to write it is N.
terms.example: A small apple of about 100 grams pulls down on your hand with about 1 newton.
terms.art: An apple on an open palm, with '1 N' written beside it.

terms.meaning: A tool that shows how big a pull is. It has a spring inside, a hook at the bottom and a scale of numbers. People also call it a spring balance or a newton meter.
terms.example: Hook a school bag on a forcemeter. The pointer shows how hard the bag pulls down.
terms.art: A see-through forcemeter showing the spring, the hook, the pointer and the numbers.

terms.meaning: A coil of wire that stretches when you pull it and goes back when you let go. A bigger pull makes it stretch further.
terms.example: There is a spring inside a ballpoint pen. Many doors have a long spring to pull them shut.
terms.art: A coiled spring short and relaxed, then long and stretched with a hand pulling.

terms.meaning: The row of marks and numbers on a tool such as a ruler or a forcemeter. You read the number where the pointer stops.
terms.example: The scale on a ruler has centimetres. The scale on a forcemeter has newtons.
terms.art: A close-up of a forcemeter scale with big numbers and small marks between them.

terms.meaning: The line or arrow on a forcemeter or a dial that moves to show the reading.
terms.example: On a forcemeter, the pointer slides down the scale as you pull harder.
terms.art: A red pointer line sitting on the 3 mark of a scale.

terms.meaning: The number you read on a tool such as a forcemeter, with its unit.
terms.example: The reading on the forcemeter is 4 newtons.
terms.art: A child's eye level with a forcemeter, reading the number.

terms.meaning: The starting mark on a scale. Before you start, the pointer must sit exactly on zero.
terms.example: With nothing on the hook, the pointer should point to 0.
terms.art: An empty forcemeter with its pointer exactly on 0 and a green tick.

terms.meaning: The smallest and the biggest force a tool can show. Pulling harder than its range can spoil the spring.
terms.example: A 0 to 10 newton forcemeter is good for an apple, but not for a bucket of water.
terms.art: Two forcemeters, one marked 0 to 10 N and one marked 0 to 100 N.

terms.meaning: To put the marks on a tool by testing it with things you already know.
terms.example: You hang a 100 gram packet on your homemade forcemeter. You mark that place '1 N', because 100 grams pulls with about 1 newton.
terms.art: A rubber band forcemeter with a packet hanging and a hand drawing the 1 N mark.

terms.meaning: A careful guess of a size, made before you test.
terms.example: I estimate my water bottle pulls with about 5 newtons, because it feels like five apples. Then I test it.
terms.art: A child thinking with a bubble showing '5 N?' next to a water bottle.

terms.meaning: The pull of a planet on a thing. Weight is a force, so scientists count it in newtons.
terms.example: A 1 kilogram packet of atta has a weight of about 10 newtons on Earth.
terms.art: A packet of atta hanging from a forcemeter reading 10 N, an arrow pointing down to the Earth.

terms.meaning: How much stuff a thing is made of. It is counted in grams and kilograms. Your mass is the same on Earth and on the Moon.
terms.example: A packet of salt with a mass of 1 kilogram has the same salt in it everywhere.
terms.art: The same packet of salt on Earth and on the Moon, labelled 1 kg in both.

terms.meaning: A tool that shows how hard things press down. Kitchen scales and bathroom scales are weighing scales. In India they show grams and kilograms.
terms.example: You stand on a bathroom scale and it shows 25 kilograms.
terms.art: A bathroom scale with two small feet on it and a dial.

terms.meaning: A small block of metal inside digital scales. It bends a tiny bit when pressed. A chip turns that bend into a number.
terms.example: The digital scale at the vegetable shop has a load cell under its tray.
terms.art: A cut-away digital scale showing a metal block bending slightly under a tray of tomatoes.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle in the outer part of every atom. Electrons push other electrons away.
terms.example: When you push a door, the electrons in your hand push the electrons in the door away. That is the push you feel.
terms.art: A hand pressing a door, with a zoom circle showing fuzzy electron clouds of the hand and the door pushing apart.

terms.meaning: A tiny group of atoms joined together. Atoms are the tiny building blocks of everything.
terms.example: Inside your body, some molecules walk along threads, pulling loads like porters.
terms.art: A cartoon of a two-legged molecule walking along a thread inside a cell, carrying a bubble.

terms.meaning: The pull that every thing has on every other thing. The Earth's gravity pulls you down. The Moon's gravity pulls the sea.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a mango down from the tree.
terms.art: A mango falling from a tree with an arrow pointing to the ground.

explanations.concept: A unit is one small pull, counted again and again
explanations.definition: To put a number on a pull, choose one small pull that never changes. Then count how many of them match the big pull. That small pull is your unit.
explanations.description: In the coin-pull test, each coin of one kind pulls down on the cup by the same amount. So 'six coins' means 'six of the same small pull'. That is all a unit is. You can choose almost anything, as long as it stays the same every time. Coins of one kind work. A mix of coins and buttons does not, because a button pulls less than a coin. People have always done this. Indian goldsmiths used the bright red seed of the gunja plant as a tiny unit of weight, called a ratti. One ratti is a little more than a tenth of a gram. Some jewellers still say 'ratti' today. Gunja seeds are poisonous if chewed, so never put one in your mouth.
examples: Six five-rupee coins started the notebook sliding. The unit was 'one five-rupee coin'.
Counting your steps across a room uses 'one of my steps' as a unit of length.
A ratti seed was a unit of weight for gold. People chose these seeds because they look very alike.
explanations.art: A row of bright red gunja seeds beside a row of identical coins, and a notebook pulled by a cup of coins.
explanations.context: In the coin-pull test, you counted coins to put a number on a pull. This card explains why that works.

explanations.concept: Why two careful people get different numbers
explanations.definition: A number means nothing without its unit. Six big coins and twelve small coins can be exactly the same pull.
explanations.description: In the coin-pull test, you and a grown-up may get different numbers for the same notebook. Both of you can be right. You were counting different small pulls. To compare, you have to find how many of one unit make the other. It is like changing rupees into dollars. Now imagine every town using its own coins, buttons or stones. Nobody could compare a pull in Pune with a pull in Patna. A builder could not order a rope strong enough for a bridge. That is why people agreed to share one unit of force.
examples: Suppose one five-rupee coin pulls as hard as two one-rupee coins. Then 6 big coins match 12 small ones.
A grown-up's step is longer than yours. The room is the same, but the number of steps is not.
Old Indian markets used the ser. But a ser in one town was often not the same as a ser in the next.
explanations.art: A child and a grown-up at the same table, the child's cup holding six big coins and the grown-up's cup holding twelve small ones, both pulling the same notebook.
explanations.context: Did you and a grown-up get different coin numbers for the same notebook? This card explains why both can be right.

explanations.concept: The newton: one unit the whole world shares
explanations.definition: Scientists everywhere count force in newtons. The short way to write newtons is N. One newton is about the pull of a small apple on your hand.
explanations.description: The newton is named after Isaac Newton, an English scientist. In a book of 1687, he explained how forces change movement. Countries agreed to call the unit 'the newton' in 1948. One newton is a small force. A small apple, or a 100 gram packet of tea, pulls on your hand with about 1 newton. So does 100 millilitres of water. A 1 litre bottle of water pulls with about 10 newtons. The newton is not something you can dig up or find in nature. It is an agreement. Because everyone keeps the same agreement, a pull in Pune and a pull in Paris can be compared.
examples: A 100 gram packet of biscuits pulls down with about 1 newton.
A 1 litre bottle of water pulls down with about 10 newtons.
A Class 3 child who is 25 kilograms presses down on the floor with about 250 newtons.
explanations.art: A row of three things on outstretched hands: a small apple labelled 1 N, a water bottle labelled 10 N, and a child standing on a scale labelled 250 N.
explanations.context: You invented your own unit of pull. This card is about the unit that the whole world agreed to share, the newton.

chart.title: How hard some everyday things pull down on your hand
chart.note: Rough sizes on Earth. Every 100 grams pulls down with about 1 newton.

explanations.definition: A force changes how something moves, or changes its shape. A force is not needed to keep something moving.
explanations.description: About 2,350 years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle taught that things need a push to keep moving. Stop pushing a cart, and it stops. For about 2,000 years, most people agreed. Then Galileo Galilei, in Italy in the early 1600s, rolled balls down a slope and onto a smooth floor. The smoother the floor, the further the ball rolled. He reasoned that on a perfectly smooth floor it would roll for ever. The cart stops because friction pulls back on it, not because the push runs out. In 1687, Isaac Newton wrote this down as a rule. A force changes movement. This gave a way to say exactly how big a force is. One newton is the push that makes a 1 kilogram thing speed up by 1 metre per second, every second. This works only if nothing rubs or pulls back.
examples: A bigger kick makes the same football speed up faster.
The same push makes an empty trolley speed up much more than a full one.
In space, where nothing rubs, a gentle push keeps a floating astronaut moving until something stops her.
explanations.art: A ball rolling down a wooden slope onto a long smooth floor, and beside it a ball floating among stars with dotted lines showing it getting faster each second.
explanations.context: What is a force, and how do scientists decide how big one newton is? This card explains what a force does to movement.

explanations.definition: A forcemeter is a spring with a hook and a scale. The bigger the pull on the hook, the further the spring stretches. The pointer moves further along the scale.
explanations.description: Look inside a forcemeter and you find a spring. The top of the spring is fixed. The hook hangs from the bottom. When something pulls on the hook, the spring stretches, and a pointer fixed to it slides down the scale. Twice the pull gives twice the stretch. That is why the marks on a forcemeter are evenly spaced. An English scientist, Robert Hooke, published this rule in 1678. The marks are put on by hanging things whose pull is already agreed, such as 100 gram packets. So every forcemeter carries the shared unit inside it. A spring only follows the rule if you don't pull too hard. Pull past its range and it stays stretched, and the forcemeter is spoiled.
examples: A luggage scale at the airport is a forcemeter for heavy bags.
A shopkeeper's hanging spring balance for vegetables is a forcemeter marked in kilograms.
You can make a forcemeter with a rubber band, a paper clip and a strip of card.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a forcemeter: the fixed top, the spring, the pointer and the hook, shown twice, with 1 N and then 2 N hanging and the spring twice as long.
explanations.context: A forcemeter turns a pull into a number of newtons. This card shows what is inside, and why it works.

explanations.definition: To read a forcemeter well, check the zero and hold it straight. Pull steadily and read at eye level. Count the small marks and write the unit.
explanations.description: A forcemeter gives a true number only if you use it well. First, check the zero. With nothing on the hook, the pointer must be exactly on 0. If it isn't, turn the little screw at the top until it is. Second, hold it straight and still. A swinging bag gives a wobbly reading. Third, pull slowly and steadily. A sudden jerk makes the pointer jump too high. Fourth, look at the pointer with your eyes level with it, not from above or below. Fifth, count the small marks between the big numbers. Last, write the number with its unit, for example '3 newtons'.
examples: If the pointer starts at 1 with nothing on it, every reading will be 1 newton too big.
Reading from above or below can make the pointer seem to sit on the wrong mark.
A 0 to 10 newton forcemeter with 20 small marks has one mark for every half newton.
explanations.art: Six small pictures: pointer on zero, holding straight, pulling slowly, eyes level with pointer, counting marks, writing '3 N'.
explanations.context: You have a forcemeter in your hand. This card explains the six habits that make its readings true.

chart.title: A forcemeter scale. Each small mark is half a newton.
chart.label: The pointer is on 3 and a half newtons.

explanations.definition: Weight is the pull of a planet on a thing. It is a force, counted in newtons. Mass is how much stuff a thing has, counted in kilograms.
explanations.description: When you hang a bag from a forcemeter, what is pulling it down? It is the Earth. The pull of a planet on a thing is called its weight. So weight is a force, and scientists count it in newtons. In shops, we say a bag of rice 'weighs 1 kilogram'. Strictly, the kilogram tells us how much rice there is. Scientists call that its mass. On Earth, every kilogram is pulled down with about 10 newtons. On the Moon, gravity is weaker. The same bag of rice would pull the forcemeter down only about one sixth as hard. The rice has not changed. Only the pull has. The unit on Weight and mass goes deeper into this.
examples: A 1 kilogram bag of rice reads about 10 newtons on Earth, and about 1.6 newtons on the Moon.
Astronauts on the Moon could carry heavy packs easily, because their packs pulled down less.
On Jupiter, the same bag of rice would pull down about two and a half times harder than on Earth.
explanations.art: The same bag of rice hanging from a forcemeter on the Moon, the Earth and Jupiter, with the pointer lower each time.
explanations.context: When you weigh a bag on a forcemeter, what is pulling it down? This card explains that weight is a force.

explanations.concept: Putting a number on a push
explanations.definition: Weighing scales put a number on pushes. A spring or a bending metal block inside turns the push into a number.
explanations.description: A forcemeter shows pulls. So how do we put a number on a push? A bathroom scale is one answer. When you stand on it, you push down on it. Inside an old scale is a spring that gets squashed. Inside a digital scale is a load cell. That is a small block of metal that bends a tiny bit when pressed. A chip turns the bend into a number. Scales in India show kilograms, not newtons. To turn the kilograms on a scale into newtons of push, multiply by 10. You can also see pushes without numbers. A balloon, a sponge or a ball of foam squashes more when the push is bigger.
examples: Pressing a bathroom scale with one finger might show 2 kilograms. That is a push of about 20 newtons.
A punching game at a fair shows how hard a punch hits its pad.
Car makers crash cars into walls fitted with sensors, to find how big the push is and make cars safer.
explanations.art: A child pressing a bathroom scale with one finger, then with both palms, the dial higher in the second picture.
explanations.context: A forcemeter shows pulls. This card is about how we put a number on pushes, from bathroom scales to squashed balloons.

explanations.definition: When you push something, the electrons on the outside of your atoms push the electrons of its atoms away. Almost every push and pull you feel is this one electric force.
explanations.description: Zoom in on your finger pressing a table. Your skin and the table are both made of atoms. Each atom has electrons on its outside. Electrons push other electrons away. So your finger never quite touches the table. The electrons push apart, and that push is what you feel. A string pulling a cup is the same force. The atoms of the string hold on to each other, so a pull at one end reaches the other. A spring, the grip of friction and the push of the wind are this force too. Even a forcemeter's spring works this way: its atoms pull back on their neighbours when you stretch it. In everyday life, only the pull of gravity is different. So the grip you measured in the coin test is the push and pull of trillions of electrons.
examples: Press your palm on a table. The push you feel is electrons pushing electrons.
The string in the coin test pulls because its atoms hold on to their neighbours.
The weight of the coins comes from gravity, the one everyday force that is not electric.
explanations.art: A finger pressing a table, with a zoom circle showing the fuzzy electron clouds of the skin and the table pushing apart, never quite touching.
explanations.context: When you push something, what is really happening? This card zooms in to the atoms.

explanations.definition: Forces range from far less than one newton to many millions of newtons. The newton works for all of them.
explanations.description: Forces in our world go from unbelievably tiny to unbelievably huge. A sheet of paper pulls down with about one twentieth of a newton. A grown-up presses on the floor with about 600 newtons. A big saltwater crocodile, like the ones in Bhitarkanika in Odisha, can bite with about 16,000 newtons. The giant Saturn V rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon pushed off with about 34 million newtons. And the Earth and the Moon pull on each other with about 200 million million million newtons. Scientists count all of them in the same unit, the newton.
examples: A one-rupee coin pulls down with only a few hundredths of a newton.
An Asian elephant weighs about 40,000 newtons.
India's rockets, at Sriharikota, push off with millions of newtons.
explanations.art: A tall ladder of pictures from a paper sheet at the bottom, through an apple, a child, a car and an elephant, to a rocket and the Earth and Moon at the top.
explanations.context: How small and how big can a force be? This card climbs the ladder of forces, from a sheet of paper to the Moon.

explanations.concept: The tiniest forces, inside living things
explanations.definition: Scientists can detect forces far smaller than a newton, using light beams and tiny bending needles.
explanations.description: Inside every cell in your body, tiny molecules walk along threads, carrying loads. They are like porters on a mountain path. One kind is called kinesin. How hard can one kinesin molecule pull? To find out, scientists used light as a pair of tweezers. A focused laser beam can hold a tiny bead and show how hard something tugs on it. These are called optical tweezers. Arthur Ashkin invented them, and won a Nobel Prize for them in 2018. He shared that prize with Gérard Mourou and Donna Strickland, who found how to make very short, strong laser flashes. Strickland was only the third woman ever to win the Nobel Prize in Physics. With optical tweezers, scientists found that one kinesin molecule pulls with about 6 piconewtons. That is about 6 millionths of a millionth of a newton. Other scientists use a tiny needle that bends, called an atomic force microscope. It feels the push of single atoms.
examples: Your muscles work because millions of molecules each give a tiny pull at the same time.
An atomic force microscope can feel the bumps of single atoms on a surface.
Optical tweezers can stretch a single strand of DNA, the molecule that carries your body's instructions.
explanations.art: A glowing laser beam holding a tiny bead, tied to a two-legged molecule walking along a thread inside a cell.
explanations.context: Can we put a number on forces too small to feel at all? This card goes inside your body, to forces a million million times smaller than an apple's pull.

explanations.concept: Weighing the Earth with a twisting wire
explanations.definition: Cavendish measured the tiny gravity pull between lead balls with a twisting wire, in 1798. It let scientists work out the mass of the Earth.
explanations.description: Everything pulls on everything else with gravity. Even two balls on a table pull each other. But that pull is so tiny that nobody could feel it. In 1798, an English scientist, Henry Cavendish, measured it. He hung a rod with two small lead balls from a thin wire. He put two big lead balls nearby. The big balls pulled the small ones, and the wire twisted a tiny bit. The twisting wire worked like a very gentle forcemeter. The pull was tiny, about the weight of one fine grain of sand. Cavendish watched through a telescope from outside the room, so even the warmth of his body would not spoil it. From this, scientists could work out how heavy the whole Earth is. The idea and the first apparatus came from another scientist, John Michell. He died in 1793, before he could use it.
examples: A twisting wire can show forces far too small for a spring.
Cavendish's measurement let people work out the mass of the Earth for the first time.
explanations.art: A dark wooden shed, inside a rod with two small balls hanging on a wire, two big balls beside them, and a telescope poking through the wall.
explanations.context: How do you put a number on a pull that is smaller than a grain of sand's weight? This card is about how one experiment weighed the Earth.

explanations.concept: Who decides how big a unit is?
explanations.definition: Since 2019, the kilogram, and so the newton, is fixed by numbers from nature, not by one metal object.
explanations.description: A newton depends on the kilogram, the metre and the second. So who decides how big a kilogram is? From 1889 to 2019, the kilogram was one real metal cylinder, made of platinum and iridium. It was kept locked in a vault near Paris, under three glass covers. People called it Le Grand K. By agreement, it was exactly 1 kilogram, whatever happened to it. Countries had copies. India's copy is kept at the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi. But over about 100 years, the copies and the original slowly drifted apart, by about 50 millionths of a gram. Nobody could say which had changed. So in 2018, at a meeting in Versailles in France, countries voted to change the rule. Since 20 May 2019, the kilogram is fixed by a constant of nature, called the Planck constant. Even here there is an agreement. People chose the exact number for it, so the new kilogram matched the old one. A machine called a Kibble balance can turn that number into a real kilogram. It balances a weight against the push of a magnet on an electric current. Bryan Kibble, a British scientist, invented it in 1975.
examples: The metre is now fixed by the speed of light, not by a metal bar.
A country with a Kibble balance can now make its own kilogram, without visiting Paris.
explanations.art: A shiny metal cylinder under three glass bell jars, and beside it a tall modern machine with a magnet and a pan.
explanations.context: Every forcemeter is checked against an agreed kilogram. This card is about who keeps the kilogram, and why that changed in 2019.

explanations.definition: Fair trade needs weights everyone agrees on. India has used standard weights since the Indus Valley cities, about 4,500 years ago.
explanations.description: People have needed fair weights for thousands of years. About 4,500 years ago, traders in the Indus Valley cities used stone weights. They were carefully cut into little cubes. The sizes followed a pattern: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64, and then bigger steps. The same sizes were used in cities hundreds of kilometres apart. Much later came the Arthashastra, an old Indian book about running a kingdom. It describes an officer who checked the scales and weights in markets. For a long time, India used units like the tola, the ser and the maund. They were not the same everywhere. In 1958, India began to change to grams and kilograms. Today, Legal Metrology officers still check shop scales and put a seal on honest ones.
examples: Indus Valley stone weights have been found at Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Lothal.
Some grandparents still say 'one ser of milk' or 'one tola of gold'.
Look for a small seal or stamp on the scales at your vegetable shop.
explanations.art: A row of small polished stone cubes of doubling sizes on a cloth, beside a modern digital shop scale with a stamp on it.
explanations.context: Why do fair weights matter? This card goes back 4,500 years, to India's first standard weights.

explanations.description: We can put very exact numbers on forces. But what is a force, deep down? How does the Earth pull a mango without touching it? Scientists have given different answers, and the question is not finished.
examples: A magnet pulls a pin across a gap. Nothing we can see joins them.
A forcemeter inside a falling lift would read zero, even though gravity is still there.

perspectives.explanation: A force is whatever changes how a thing moves. Newton worked out exactly how gravity pulls. But he said he did not know how it reaches across empty space, and he would not guess.
Gravity is not really a pull at all. Heavy things bend space and time around them. Other things follow the bends. A forcemeter in a falling lift reads zero, because nothing is holding the bag up.
Electric and magnetic forces are carried by tiny particles flying between things. Many think gravity might be carried by a particle too, called a graviton. Nobody has ever found one.

explanations.art: A mango falling from a tree, with three thought bubbles: invisible strings, a curved sheet, and tiny particles flying between Earth and mango.
explanations.context: We can count forces in newtons. This card asks a harder question that scientists still argue about: what is a force?

explanations.concept: Does measuring change what you measure?
explanations.description: A heavy forcemeter adds its own pull to what it measures. A cold thermometer cools the tea a tiny bit. Scientists always try to make their tools disturb things as little as possible. But at the size of atoms, there seems to be a limit. Quantum physics, the science of the very tiniest things, says that measuring something always nudges it a little. In 2014, physicists in California measured a force of about 42 yoctonewtons. One yoctonewton is so small that a million million million million of them make just one newton. They found their measurement was close to that limit. Whether we can ever beat it, in clever ways, is still being worked on.
examples: A spring balance hanging on a spring balance adds its own weight to the reading.
Shining light on a tiny thing to see it also gives it a tiny push.

perspectives.explanation: There is a limit to how gently you can measure. It comes from quantum physics.
Clever tricks can get past the usual limit in some experiments. How far this can go is still being explored.

explanations.art: A tiny glowing cloud of atoms, a laser beam touching it, and a magnifying glass with a question mark.
explanations.context: Every measurement disturbs things a little. This card follows that idea down to the smallest force ever measured.

agreed.text: Forces are counted in newtons, all over the world.
agreed.evidence: Countries agreed to name the unit 'newton' in 1948. Every science book and forcemeter in the world uses it.
agreed.context: This card is about the unit that scientists everywhere use for force.

agreed.text: A number tells you nothing until you know its unit.
agreed.evidence: In the coin-pull test, the same notebook needed 6 big coins or 12 small coins. In 1999, a space probe called the Mars Climate Orbiter was lost. One team had worked in newtons, and another in an older unit, the pound-force.
agreed.context: This card is about why every number needs its unit.

agreed.text: A spring stretches evenly as the pull grows, until you pull it too hard.
agreed.evidence: Hang 100 gram packets on a spring one at a time. Each packet adds about the same stretch. Robert Hooke published this in 1678.
agreed.context: This card is about why forcemeters can have evenly spaced marks.

agreed.text: On Earth, every kilogram is pulled down with about 10 newtons. More exactly, it is 9.8 newtons.
agreed.evidence: Hang a 1 kilogram packet on a good forcemeter. It reads just under 10 newtons. Scientists have checked this very carefully all over the planet.
agreed.context: This card links kilograms, the unit on shop packets, to newtons, the unit of force.

agreed.text: The same thing has a smaller weight on the Moon, but the same mass.
agreed.evidence: From 1969 to 1972, astronauts on the Moon bounced along with heavy packs. On Earth those packs would have been hard to carry. Their packs still held the same stuff.
agreed.context: This card is about why weight, a force, depends on where you are.

chart.title: A 30 kilogram child's weight on the Earth and on the Moon

agreed.text: Scales and forcemeters must be checked against agreed standards to be fair.
agreed.evidence: In India, Legal Metrology officers test shop scales with standard weights and seal the honest ones. Scientists check their own tools against national standards, like the kilogram copy kept in New Delhi.
agreed.context: This card is about why a scale is only fair if someone checks it.

challenging.claim: Things need a push to keep moving.
challenging.who: Aristotle, about 2,350 years ago, and most people without thinking about it
challenging.for: A cart stops when the bullock stops pulling. A ball stops rolling. Everything we see seems to need a push to keep going.
challenging.against: Galileo saw that a ball rolls further on a smoother floor. Things stop because friction and air pull back on them. In space, where nothing rubs, a spacecraft keeps moving for years with its engines off.
challenging.context: For about 2,000 years, people believed that a force is needed to keep things moving. This card looks at that idea.

challenging.claim: A number tells you the true size of a thing, all by itself.
challenging.for: Numbers look exact. '12' seems to say exactly how big the pull is.
challenging.against: The same notebook needed 6 big coins or 12 small coins. A number only says how many units fit. Until 2019 even the kilogram was simply whatever one metal cylinder weighed.
challenging.context: You counted coins to put a number on a pull. This card asks whether a number means anything without its unit.

challenging.claim: If nothing moves, there is no force.
challenging.who: Many children, and many grown-ups without noticing
challenging.for: We usually notice forces when something starts moving.
challenging.against: Push hard on a wall through a balloon. The wall doesn't move, but the balloon squashes flat. A book lying on a table is pulled down by the Earth. At the same time, the table pushes it up. Put a bathroom scale under it and you can see the push as a number.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that a force only exists when something moves.

challenging.claim: Your hands can tell you exactly how heavy something is.
challenging.who: A common belief. Many traders once judged loads by lifting them.
challenging.for: With practice, people get quite good at guessing weights.
challenging.against: Tired arms make things feel heavier. A small box feels heavier than a big box of the same weight. Augustin Charpentier, a French doctor, wrote about this in 1891. That is why fair trade uses scales.
challenging.context: This card is about whether lifting something is a good way to tell how heavy it is.

challenging.claim: A bathroom scale measures how much of you there is.
challenging.who: Most people, most of the time
challenging.for: The scale shows kilograms, and kilograms measure mass, the amount of stuff.
challenging.against: The scale really shows how hard you push down on it. Bend your knees fast and the number jumps. Press on a table beside you and it drops. On the Moon it would show a much smaller number, though you'd still be all there. The scale is just set to turn your push into kilograms, as if you were standing still on Earth.
challenging.context: You stand on a bathroom scale and read a number. This card asks what that number really measures.

challenging.claim: Isaac Newton worked out the rules of forces all by himself.
challenging.for: Newton's book of 1687 brought the rules together in one place, and the unit of force is named after him.
challenging.against: Newton built on Galileo, Kepler and others. Robert Hooke wrote to Newton about how gravity might weaken with distance, and felt Newton gave him too little credit. Newton himself wrote that he stood 'on the shoulders of giants'.
challenging.context: The unit of force is named after Isaac Newton. This card asks how much of the credit was his alone.

challenging.claim: Gravity is a force, just like a pull on a rope.
challenging.who: Newton's way of seeing it, still used in most science books
challenging.for: It works for nearly everything, from dropping mangoes to sending rockets to the Moon.
challenging.against: Albert Einstein showed in 1915 that gravity can be seen as bent space and time. A forcemeter falling freely reads zero. His view explains some things Newton's can't, like a slow wobble in the orbit of the planet Mercury.
challenging.context: This card is about whether gravity is really a force at all.

big_questions.q: You and a grown-up got different numbers for one notebook's pull. Can two different numbers both be true?
big_questions.hint: Think about 6 big coins and 12 small coins. What stayed the same?

big_questions.q: If people had never invented the newton, would the notebook still need the same pull?
big_questions.hint: Would a mango still fall if nobody had a word for force?

big_questions.q: Is a number something we find in the world, or something we bring to it?
big_questions.hint: Where did your number for the notebook come from: the notebook, the coins, or you?

big_questions.q: Before 2019, the kilogram was one lump of metal. If a speck of dust landed on it, did the lump get heavier? Or did everything else get a little lighter?
big_questions.hint: By the rule of that time, the lump was always exactly 1 kilogram, whatever happened to it.

big_questions.q: Why does a stack of two notebooks need about twice the pull to start sliding? What is happening where the notebook touches the table?
big_questions.hint: Zoom in. The cover and the table both have tiny bumps. What does a heavier stack do to them?

big_questions.q: Why can we trust a spring more than our hands?
big_questions.hint: Does a spring get tired, or expect a big box to be heavy?

big_questions.q: Your hands were fooled by the big and small boxes. What else might our senses get wrong?
big_questions.hint: Think about how warm water feels after your hands were in ice.

big_questions.q: How does the Earth pull a mango without touching it?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have three different answers. None of them is the final word.

big_questions.q: Is there a smallest possible force? Is there a biggest?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have measured a force of 42 yoctonewtons. And the pull near a black hole is beyond anything on our ladder.

big_questions.q: On the Moon you would weigh much less but still be all of you. So what is the real 'you': your weight, or something else?
big_questions.hint: What stays the same about you everywhere you go?

story.title: Ten Packets of Salt
story.note: Made up. The village, Pushpa, Basanti, Mohan Lal, Diwan and Kamla Didi are imagined. Porters really do carry loads on mountain treks in Uttarakhand, often paid by the load. Spring balances really have a zero screw that can be set wrongly. Sealed packets must by law weigh what they say, and Legal Metrology officers check scales.
text: In the mountains of Uttarakhand, a stony path climbs from a small village all the way to a glacier, a river of ice. Every spring, trekkers came from the cities to walk it. They brought tents and cooking pots, sacks of rice and tins of ghee. They did not carry these things themselves. The porters of the village did.

Pushpa was nine. Her mother, Basanti, was a porter. Each morning, before the sun climbed over the ridge, Pushpa walked with her to the walnut tree at the edge of the village. There the contractor, Mohan Lal, weighed the loads. He had a brass spring balance as long as his forearm. Inside it was a coiled spring. When a basket hung from its hook, the spring stretched, and a little pointer slid down a row of numbers.

Mohan Lal paid the porters by the kilo. 'Fifteen,' he would call, squinting at the pointer as a basket swung below it. 'Eighteen. Fourteen.' His clerk wrote every number in a long book. At the end of the season, the porters would be paid for every kilo in the book.

Basanti bent and slipped the strap of her basket over her forehead. She stood, and the basket rose onto her back. Pushpa saw her mother's neck go tight, and her knees tremble for a moment before they steadied.
'Fourteen,' said Mohan Lal.
That evening, Basanti sat by the fire and rubbed her neck. 'Fourteen,' she said softly. 'It felt like twenty-five.'
'Maybe you were tired, Ma,' said Pushpa.
'Maybe,' said her mother. 'A tired back is a poor judge. And Mohan Lal's balance is made of brass. Brass does not get tired.'

But Pushpa kept thinking. All the porters were saying the same thing. Old Diwan, who had carried loads for thirty years, said the baskets had grown heavier, or else he had grown weaker. The young men said nothing at all. They did not want to sound weak.

The next morning, Pushpa stood very close to the walnut tree. Mohan Lal hung his balance from a low branch, with nothing on the hook. Pushpa looked at the pointer. Then she looked again. It was not on the zero. It sat a little way above the zero, in the empty space at the top where there were no numbers at all.
She tugged her mother's sleeve. 'Ma, the pointer is in the wrong place.'
Basanti glanced at Mohan Lal and hushed her. 'Don't make trouble, beti.'
Mohan Lal laughed. 'So the little one wants to read my balance! Go and play.' His thumb slid across the brass. When Pushpa looked again, she could not see the pointer at all.

All day, she turned it over in her mind. A balance gives you a number. But how do you check the balance? You would need something whose weight everybody already agreed on. Something nobody could argue with.

Then she thought of Kamla Didi's tea shop. Kamla Didi sold salt in sealed packets. Each one was printed with the words 1 kg. They came from a factory far away, and by law every packet had to hold what it said. Every family in the village had cooked with that salt for years.
That evening, Pushpa stood at the tea shop counter. 'Didi, I don't want to buy salt,' she said. 'I want to borrow it. Only until tomorrow morning.'
Kamla Didi raised her eyebrows. Then, without asking why, she counted ten packets into a cloth bag. 'Ten packets. Ten kilos,' she said. 'Bring back every one.'

The bag was so heavy that Pushpa had to carry it in her arms, like a sleeping baby goat. It was heavier than her school bag full of books. By the time she reached the walnut tree, her arms were aching and the porters were already lining up.
'Mohan Lal-ji,' she said, loud enough for everyone to hear. 'Please weigh my load.'
The porters laughed, kindly. Mohan Lal laughed too. He hooked her bag onto his balance and peered at it. 'Five kilos,' he said. 'A little girl's little load.'
'There are ten packets of salt in that bag,' said Pushpa. Her voice shook, but she kept going. 'Each one says one kilo. Kamla Didi sold them. All of you have cooked with them.'
She tipped the packets out onto a blanket, one at a time. The porters began to count with her. One. Two. Three. By the end, the whole line was counting. 'Eight. Nine. Ten.'

Nobody spoke. Then old Diwan stepped forward. He lifted the brass balance off the branch and held it up to the morning light, with nothing on its hook. Everyone could see the pointer now, sitting high in the empty space above the zero.
'Five kilos missing from a bag of ten,' Diwan said slowly. 'And five from my basket. Every morning. For how long?'

Mohan Lal began to say that factories cheat too, that the packets were probably light. But just then Kamla Didi came up the path. She was carrying her own shop balance, the old kind with two pans and iron weights. She set it on a flat rock. She put five packets of salt in one pan and a five-kilo iron weight in the other. The pans swung, and settled, and hung perfectly level.
Two different ways of weighing. And they agreed.
Mohan Lal did not look at anybody. He turned a small screw at the top of his balance, and the pointer slid down until it sat exactly on the zero. Then he hooked on Basanti's basket.
'Nineteen,' he said quietly.

That season, every porter put a few rupees into a tin. At the end of the summer, they bought their own spring balance from the town. They hung it on a nail on the walnut tree. And every morning after that, before the first basket went on the hook, somebody would call out across the cold air: 'Pushpa! Check the zero!' And Pushpa would look, and nod, and the weighing would begin.
story.epiphany: A spring balance is a forcemeter. It turns a pull into a number by stretching a spring. But the number is only fair if the balance agrees with something everyone already trusts. Pushpa does what scientists call calibrating. She tests the balance with ten packets whose weight everybody has agreed on. Then a second, different balance agrees with them. Her mother's tired back could not prove anything, because a feeling belongs to one person. Ten sealed packets belonged to everyone. That is the whole idea of a unit: a number means something only because people share what it counts. The story also quietly asks who is believed, and who carries the load.
ask: Basanti said her basket felt like twenty-five kilos. Why couldn't her feeling prove that the balance was wrong?
What was wrong with Mohan Lal's balance before anything was hung on it?
Why did Pushpa choose sealed packets of salt to test the balance? Why not stones from the path?
Kamla Didi checked the salt with a different kind of balance. Why did it matter that two different tools agreed?
Why do you think the porters asked Pushpa to check the zero every morning, and not Mohan Lal?
Why didn't the young porters say anything about the heavy loads at first?

games.title: Guess the Newtons
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the grown-up's guesses
games.context: This is an estimating game. Players guess how hard everyday things pull down, in newtons, and then check with a forcemeter. The closest guess wins points.

printables.title: 20 thing cards to cut out
items: A full steel tumbler of water
A tiffin box with lunch in it
A MYSTERY BAG: a grown-up secretly fills a bag. Guess first!
YOUR CHOICE: pick anything that fits in a bag

printables.title: The newton helper strip
items: 5 N: half a litre of water
20 N: a full school bag, about

rules: Cut out the 20 thing cards. Shuffle them and put them face down.
Hang a bag with handles from the forcemeter. Check that the pointer is on zero with the empty bag. If it isn't, write down the empty reading and take it away each time.
On your turn, turn over a card. Find that thing at home.
Every player holds the thing in their hand and writes a guess in newtons. Use the newton helper strip to help.
Put the thing in the bag and read the forcemeter. Write the real number.
The closest guess wins 2 points. A guess within 1 newton wins 1 extra point.
After 10 cards, add up the points. The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Put out the forcemeter, a cloth bag with handles and the score sheet. 2. Shuffle the thing cards face down. 3. Hold up a small apple and say it pulls with about 1 newton.
flow.say: Hold this apple. Feel how it pulls your hand down. That is about 1 newton. We will use it to help us guess other things.
flow.kid: Hold the apple. Feel it pull your hand down. That pull is about 1 newton. Remember how it feels.
flow.context: This is the first step of Guess the Newtons. You learn what 1 newton feels like, so you can guess other things.
flow.parent: A small apple of about 100 grams pulls with about 1 newton. A 1 litre bottle of water pulls with about 10 newtons. Let your child hold both before you start.

flow.do: Hang the empty bag from the forcemeter. Ask your child to check the pointer before you begin.
flow.say: Before every game we check the zero. Where is the pointer with just the empty bag on it?
flow.kid: Hang the empty bag on the hook. Look at the pointer. Is it on zero?
flow.context: This step of Guess the Newtons checks that the forcemeter starts at zero, so every reading is fair.
flow.parent: A cloth bag weighs about half a newton. If it does, turn the zero screw with the bag on. Or take the bag's number away from each reading. Both are fair, as long as you do the same every time.

check.q: Game moment: before the first card, the referee checks the forcemeter. Where should the pointer be with only the empty bag on?
check.why: Exactly on zero. Then every reading in the game starts fair. Picking 'anywhere' usually means the pointer is seen as just a decoration. But if it starts at 1, every guess is judged against a number 1 newton too big. Picking 'the biggest number' mixes up the start of the scale with the end.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card. 2. Everyone holds the thing and writes a guess in newtons. 3. Put it in the bag and hang it on the forcemeter. 4. Read the pointer at eye level. 5. Score the guesses.
flow.say: Hold it in your hand. Compare it with the apple. Is it like two apples? Ten apples? Now write your guess.
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Find the thing. Hold it and guess its newtons. Then hang it on the forcemeter. Was your guess close?
flow.context: This is the main part of Guess the Newtons. Players guess each thing's pull in newtons, then check it on the forcemeter.

ask.q: How did you make your guess?
good: I compared it with the apple.
It felt like five apples, so I guessed 5 newtons.
It is bigger than the water bottle, so more than 10 newtons.

flow.parent: Guesses usually get better as the game goes on. That is the point. Praise the method, for example 'you compared it with the bottle', not just the closest number.

flow.do: When the mystery bag comes up, a grown-up fills a bag secretly. Players guess without looking inside, then hang it on the forcemeter.
flow.say: This one is a mystery bag. You can feel it, but you can't look inside. What do you think it pulls with?
flow.kid: Mystery bag! Don't peek. Lift it and guess the newtons. Then check it.
flow.context: This step of Guess the Newtons uses a mystery bag, filled in secret.
flow.think: Did the mystery bag feel heavier or lighter than it really was? Why might that happen?
flow.parent: Try putting something small and heavy in the bag, like a steel tumbler of coins. Small heavy things often feel heavier than they are.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then look at the score sheet together and find the guess that was furthest out.
flow.say: Who won? Now let's look for our biggest surprise. Which thing was most different from what we guessed?
flow.kid: Count the points. Who won? Which thing surprised you most?
flow.context: This is the last step of Guess the Newtons. You count the points and look for the biggest surprise.
flow.think: Why do we need a forcemeter if our guesses got quite good?

games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child alone
games.context: This is a card game about the sizes of forces. Each card shows a real force with its size in newtons. Players place the cards on a ladder from tiny to huge.

rules: Cut out the force cards. Hide the numbers by folding the bottom of each card under.
Lay the ladder on the floor, TINY at the bottom and HUGE at the top.
On your turn, take a card and read only the top part out loud.
Guess which rung it belongs on. Put it there. Then unfold the number and check.
A right guess wins 1 point. If it is on the wrong rung, move it to the right one.
When all the cards are placed, put the cards on each rung in order, smallest to biggest, together.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four rungs of the ladder on the floor in a column. 2. Fold the numbers under on every card. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: This ladder goes from tiny forces at the bottom to huge forces at the top. Let's see where every force belongs.
flow.kid: Lay the ladder on the floor. Tiny at the bottom. Huge at the top. Fold the numbers under on every card.
flow.context: This is the first step of Climb the Force Ladder. You set up a ladder that goes from tiny forces to huge ones.

flow.do: Play one practice card together: 'A 1 litre water bottle on your hand'.
flow.say: Here's a practice card. A 1 litre water bottle on your hand. Which rung?
flow.kid: Practice card: a 1 litre bottle of water on your hand. Which rung is it?
flow.context: This step of Climb the Force Ladder is a practice round with one card.

check.q: A 1 litre water bottle pulls down with about 10 newtons. Which rung of the force ladder is that?
check.why: About 10 newtons is the very bottom of the Medium rung. Picking Small usually means 10 is counted as 'up to 10'. The Small rung stops just before 10. Picking Tiny or Huge usually means the newton's size is not clear yet. Hold an apple: that is 1 newton. The bottle is about ten apples.

flow.parent: 10 newtons sits right at the start of the Medium rung. This is a good moment to explain what 'up to' means: the Small rung stops just before 10.

flow.do: Take turns. Each player reads a card, places it, then unfolds the number to check.
flow.say: Read the card. Close your eyes and imagine it. Is it tiny, small, medium or huge?
flow.kid: Read your card. Imagine that force. Put it on a rung. Then check the number.
flow.context: This is the main part of Climb the Force Ladder. Players put each force on the rung where they think it belongs.

ask.q: The molecule and the rocket are both on the ladder. How can the same unit, the newton, work for both?
good: You just use very small or very big numbers.
A newton is like a centimetre. You can count tiny parts of it or millions of it.

flow.parent: Children are often surprised that a bite or a crocodile is so far up. They are also surprised by how far down the molecule is. Both are good surprises.

flow.do: When all the cards are placed, put each rung's cards in order from smallest to biggest. Read the whole ladder from bottom to top.
flow.say: Now let's read the whole ladder from the bottom to the top, slowly. Which force surprised you most? Why?
flow.kid: Put each rung in order. Read the ladder from bottom to top. Which force amazes you most?
flow.context: This is the last step of Climb the Force Ladder. You read all the forces in order, from tiny to huge.
flow.think: Which matters more to you today: the tiny pulls inside your cells, or the huge pull of the Moon?

experiments.title: Invent a Unit: how many coins to pull a notebook?
experiments.context: This is the coin-pull investigation, the main experiment of this unit. A notebook on a table is tied to a paper cup hanging over the edge. You drop coins into the cup until the notebook starts to slide. Your unit of pull is one coin. Then you test two and three notebooks, and see what happens when a grown-up uses different coins.
experiments.question: How many coins does it take to start a notebook sliding? How does the number change for two or three notebooks? And will someone using different coins get the same number?
experiments.predict: Before you start, make three guesses, and give a reason for each one. How many coins will one notebook need, and why? Will two stacked notebooks need the same number, a few more, or twice as many? Why do you think so? Will a grown-up using a different kind of coin get the same number as you? Why or why not?
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing at a time. Use the same table, string and cup every time. In your own tests, use coins of only one kind. Put the notebook in the same place, the same way round. Drop each coin in gently, so a bump doesn't start the slide. Do every test 3 times and use the middle number, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: 3 notebooks of the same kind, thin ones with about 100 pages
about 30 coins of one kind, your heaviest kind, for example five-rupee or ten-rupee coins
about 20 coins of a lighter kind, for example one-rupee coins, for the grown-up's test. Only one kind of coin at home? The grown-up tapes coins in pairs and counts each pair as one.
a light paper or plastic cup, with two holes poked near the rim and a short loop of thread through them as a handle
about 1 metre of thin string or thread, and sticky tape
a table with a straight edge, and a cushion for the floor below it
a ruler and a round pencil, for balancing coins against each other
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes in the cup. Put a cushion under the cup, so the coins land softly when the notebook slides. Keep coins away from babies and toddlers, who might swallow them. Wash hands after handling coins.

schedule.what: Guess with reasons. Count the coins it takes to slide one, two and three notebooks. Compare with a grown-up who uses different coins. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each test: one notebook, two notebooks and three notebooks. Under the chart, write the grown-up's number for one notebook, and the kind of coin they used.

setup.caption: 1. Tape a string to the notebook. Run it over the table edge. Hang a paper cup from the other end.

setup.art: A child's hand gently dropping a coin into the hanging cup, a small pile of identical coins beside the notebook and a cushion on the floor below.
setup.caption: 2. Drop in coins one at a time. Count each one out loud.

setup.caption: 3. Stop the moment the notebook starts to slide. Write down how many coins it took.
