flow.do: 1. Put one notebook on the table. 2. Ask your child to push it gently with one finger until it slides. 3. Ask how big that push was, as a number. Do not suggest an answer.
flow.say: Push this notebook with one finger until it slides. Now tell me, how big was that push? Can you say it as a number?
flow.kid: Push the notebook with one finger until it slides. How big was your push? Can you give it a number?
flow.parent: Most children say 'small' or 'not much'. Some say a number in grams or kilograms. Ask what that number counts. The point is to feel that a push has no number on it until we choose something to count.

ask.q: What could we count, to put a number on a pull?
good: Coins.
How many things it takes to pull it.
How far a rubber band stretches.
Something that is always the same.

flow.context: This is the first step of the coin-pull investigation. You notice that a push has a size, but no number yet.

flow.do: 1. Put the notebook about 30 cm from the table edge. 2. Tape one end of the string to the middle of its front edge. 3. Run the string straight over the table edge. 4. Tie the other end to the cup's handle, so the cup hangs about 10 cm below the edge. 5. Put a cushion on the floor under the cup.
flow.say: Today the coins will do the pulling, and we will count them. Our unit of pull is one coin. Scientists named their unit after a person. What shall we call ours?
flow.kid: Tape the string to the notebook. Hang the cup over the table edge. Put a cushion underneath. Your unit is one coin. Give it a name!
flow.parent: The cup and string must be light. If the notebook slides before any coins go in, the cup is too heavy. Use a lighter cup, or a heavier notebook. Children love naming the unit after themselves, for example '1 Riya'. Use the name all through the test.
flow.context: This step of the coin-pull investigation builds the coin pull and names your own unit.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for two guesses, each with a reason. 2. Write both in the table. 3. Do not say whether they are right.
flow.say: How many coins do you think one notebook will need? Why? And two notebooks stacked: the same, a few more, or twice as many? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many coins one notebook needs. Then guess for two notebooks. Say why each time. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think two notebooks will need that many coins?
good: Two notebooks are heavier, so they press harder on the table.
It is twice the notebook, so twice the coins.
They are the same kind of notebook, so the same number.

flow.parent: Every guess with a reason is a good guess. 'The same' and 'twice as many' are both common. Keep the guesses. Your child will check them in a few minutes.
flow.context: This step of the coin-pull investigation is for guessing, with reasons, before testing.

flow.do: 1. Drop coins into the cup one at a time, gently. 2. Count out loud. 3. Stop the moment the notebook starts to slide. 4. Write the number. 5. Put the notebook back in the same place. 6. Do it 3 times in all.
flow.say: One coin at a time, gently. Count with me. Stop the moment it moves.
flow.kid: Drop in one coin at a time. Count out loud. Stop when the notebook moves. Do it 3 times.
flow.parent: The three numbers may differ by a coin or two. That is normal. Write all three and use the middle one. If a bump starts the slide early, that try doesn't count. If one notebook needs more than 12 coins, use a thinner notebook.

check.q: In the coin-pull test, your three tries were 6, 7 and 9 coins. Which number is the fairest one to use?
check.why: 7, the middle number. It sits between the others, so one odd try doesn't pull it away. Picking 22 adds the tries, but each try was one pull, not three. Picking the smallest or the biggest trusts one try more than the others.

flow.context: This is the main part of the coin-pull investigation. You count the coins it takes to start one notebook sliding.

flow.do: 1. Stack a second notebook exactly on top of the first. 2. Read out your child's guess for two notebooks. 3. Do the coin test 3 times. 4. Then stack three notebooks and test again, if you have enough coins. 5. Write every number.
flow.say: Here is your guess for two notebooks. Let's see what the coins say.
flow.kid: Stack two notebooks. Do the coin test 3 times. Then try three. Was your guess right?
flow.parent: Usually two notebooks need about twice the coins, and three need about three times. The stack presses down harder, so the tiny bumps of the cover and the table grip each other more. Don't say this yet. Let the numbers show it, and ask why at the end.
flow.think: Look at your numbers for one, two and three notebooks. Do they grow by about the same amount each time?
flow.context: This step of the coin-pull investigation tests two and three stacked notebooks.

flow.do: 1. Before you start, ask your child to guess, with a reason, whether you will get the same number. 2. Test one notebook 3 times with your different coins. 3. Your child counts. 4. Write your middle number next to theirs.
flow.say: I'm going to test one notebook with these different coins. Will I get the same number as you? Why do you think so? Now count for me.
flow.kid: Now a grown-up tests one notebook with different coins. Guess: will they get your number? Why? Then count their coins.

ask.q: We got different numbers for the same notebook. Who is right?
good: Both of us. We used different coins.
Both. My coins are heavier, so I needed fewer.
We can't compare until we know how many of your coins make one of mine.

check.q: In the coin-pull test, you needed 6 big coins to slide the notebook. A grown-up needed 12 small coins for the same notebook. What does this show?
options: The grown-up found a bigger pull
It was the same pull, counted in different units
One of you made a mistake
check.why: It was the same notebook on the same table, so it needed the same pull. The numbers differ because the coins differ. Each big coin pulls harder than a small one, so fewer were needed. Picking 'a bigger pull' means trusting a number without its unit. Picking 'a mistake' is a fair thing to check, but both counts can be right.

flow.parent: Lighter coins mean more coins for the same pull. To compare the two units, rest a ruler on a round pencil. Put one big coin on one end. Add small coins to the other end until it balances. Coins from different years weigh different amounts, so the answer may not be a whole number.
flow.context: This step of the coin-pull investigation compares your number with a grown-up's, using different coins.

flow.do: Ask what would happen if every family used its own coins, buttons or stones. Let your child answer before you say anything.
flow.say: Your cousin in another city does this test with buttons. She says 'eleven'. Is her notebook's pull bigger than ours? What would we both need, to compare?
flow.kid: Your cousin uses buttons and says 'eleven'. Is her pull bigger than yours? What would you both need?

ask.q: What would you and your cousin need, to compare your pulls?
good: The same unit.
We both use the same kind of thing.
A unit that everyone agrees on.

flow.parent: This is the reason the whole world agreed on one unit of force, the newton. Let your child say it first, in their own words. The explanation cards come after this.
flow.context: This step of the coin-pull investigation asks what happens when everyone invents a different unit.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, which numbers show it. Third, why I think it happened. Then read their guesses from step 3 together.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now, about stacking notebooks or about units? Which numbers show it? And why do you think it happened? Now let's read your first guesses. Would you change them?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think now. Which numbers show it. Why it happened. Then read your first guesses again.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: each extra notebook needs about the same number of extra coins. What I saw: one notebook took 6 coins, two took 12 and three took 17. Why: the stack presses harder on the table, so it grips more. Another good answer is about units. What I think: a number is no use without its unit. What I saw: I needed 6 coins and Amma needed 12 for the same notebook. Why: her coins were lighter.
flow.context: This is the last step of the coin-pull investigation. You say what you found, which numbers show it, and why.

experiments.title: The Pull Detective: which pull at home is biggest?
experiments.context: This is the pull detective experiment. You hook a forcemeter onto doors, drawers and bags around the home. You find how big a pull each one needs, in newtons, and compare it with your guesses.
experiments.question: Which pull at home needs the biggest force: a door, a drawer, a bag or a chair?
experiments.predict: Before you use the forcemeter, put the six pulls in order, biggest first. Say why you put the first one first and the last one last.
experiments.fair_test: Pull every thing the same way: slowly and steadily, straight along the forcemeter. Read the biggest number just as the thing starts to move. Test each pull 2 times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a forcemeter, 0 to 50 newtons, or a luggage spring scale, or your homemade forcemeter
a 30 cm piece of string tied in a loop
six things to pull: the fridge door, a drawer, a chair, a school bag, a cupboard door and a slipper
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Pull gently and slowly. Never pull a tall cupboard or bookshelf that could tip over. Don't pull past the biggest number on the forcemeter, or the spring may be spoiled.

schedule.what: Guess the order of six pulls, with reasons. Test each one twice with a forcemeter. Fill in the table and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each pull. Make each bar as tall as its biggest reading.

setup.art: A forcemeter held upright, the pointer on zero, nothing on the hook.
setup.caption: 1. Check that the pointer is on zero.

setup.art: A loop of string tied around a drawer handle, the forcemeter's hook in the loop.
setup.caption: 2. Tie a string loop to the handle. Hook the forcemeter on.
3. Pull slowly and steadily. Read the number as the drawer starts to move.
setup.art: A child pulling a kitchen drawer open with a forcemeter, eyes level with the pointer on 5 N.
A results table being filled in with a pencil, six rows.
setup.caption: 4. Write the reading in the table. Test each pull twice.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the six pulls. They are the fridge door, a drawer, a chair, a school bag, a cupboard door and a slipper. 2. Ask them to put them in order, biggest pull first. 3. Write the order in the table.
flow.say: We are going to be pull detectives. Which of these do you think needs the biggest pull? Put them in order, biggest first, and tell me why.
flow.kid: Look at the six things. Which needs the biggest pull to move? Put them in order. Say why. Write your guesses down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pull detective experiment. You guess which pull at home is biggest, before testing.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: It is heavy.
It is stuck tight.
The fridge door has a magnet that holds it shut.

flow.do: 1. Hold the forcemeter upright with nothing on the hook. 2. Ask your child to read it. 3. If the pointer is not on zero, turn the screw at the top until it is.
flow.say: Before we start, we check the zero. Look at the pointer with nothing on the hook. Is it exactly on the 0?
flow.kid: Hold the forcemeter up. Nothing on the hook. Is the pointer on 0? If not, ask a grown-up to fix it.
flow.context: This step of the pull detective experiment checks that the forcemeter starts at zero, so the readings are fair.

check.q: With nothing on the hook, your forcemeter's pointer is on 1 newton. What will happen to your readings?
options: They will all be 1 newton too big
They will all be 1 newton too small
check.why: They will all be 1 newton too big, because the pointer starts 1 newton down the scale before anything pulls. Picking 'all right' usually means the zero check seems unimportant. Picking 'too small' usually means the scale is read the wrong way round. Turn the zero screw first, or take 1 away from every reading.

flow.do: 1. Tie the string loop to the first handle. 2. Hook the forcemeter into the loop. 3. Hold it in a straight line with the pull. 4. Pull slowly and steadily. 5. Read the biggest number as the thing starts to move. 6. Do it twice and write both numbers.
flow.say: Pull slowly, like a snail. Watch the pointer climb. Tell me the biggest number just as it starts to move.
flow.kid: Hook on. Pull slowly and straight. Watch the pointer. Say the biggest number as it moves. Do it twice.
flow.context: This is the main part of the pull detective experiment. You test each pull twice with the forcemeter.
flow.parent: Keep your eyes level with the pointer when you read it. A sudden jerk makes the pointer jump too high, so the test would not be fair. For the school bag, lift it straight up off the floor slowly. If a pull goes past the end of the scale, stop, and write 'more than' the biggest number.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the biggest readings, with one bar for each pull.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each pull gets a bar. The taller the bar, the bigger the pull.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each pull. Make it as tall as its biggest number. Which bar is tallest?
flow.context: This step of the pull detective experiment turns your readings into a bar chart.

chart.title: Made-up example results: the pull needed to open or move each thing
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Compare the forcemeter's order with the guessed order in the table.
flow.say: Were your guesses right? Which pull surprised you most?
flow.kid: Look at your guesses. Look at your bars. Which one surprised you?
flow.context: This step of the pull detective experiment compares your guesses with the forcemeter's numbers.
flow.think: Why do you think the fridge door needs a bigger pull than its size suggests?
flow.parent: The fridge door often surprises children. Ask why before you explain. A magnetic strip in the rubber seal pulls the door shut.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: So, which pull was biggest? Which numbers show it? Why do you think that one needed so much?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. Which pull was biggest. Which numbers show it. Why you think so.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the fridge door needs a big pull. What I saw: it needed 18 newtons, but the drawer only needed 5. Why: there is a magnet in the fridge door pulling it shut.
flow.context: This is the last step of the pull detective experiment. You say what you found, which numbers show it, and why.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the pull needed to open or move each thing
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

experiments.title: Does the Scale Weigh You, or Your Push?
experiments.context: This is the bathroom scale experiment. You stand on a bathroom scale and change how hard you press down. How much of you there is stays the same. You watch what the number does.
experiments.question: Does a bathroom scale show how much of you there is, or how hard you push on it?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. You stand on the scale and press down on a table beside you. Will the number go up, go down or stay the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Stand in the same place on the scale each time, with both feet. Change only one thing at a time: pressing down on the table, pulling up on it, or bending your knees. Read the number each time when it settles, except for the knee test.

materials.item: a bathroom scale, spring or digital
a strong table or kitchen counter to stand beside
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up stands beside the child the whole time. Use a strong table that cannot tip. Don't jump on the scale.

schedule.what: Stand on the scale. Press down on a table, pull up on it, and bend your knees. Write what the number does.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each kilogram, write about 10 newtons beside it. Draw an arrow for your push on the scale in each picture.

setup.art: A bathroom scale on the floor beside a strong table, a child standing still on it, both hands at the sides.
setup.caption: 1. Stand still on the scale. Read the number.

setup.art: The same child pressing both palms down on the table top, the scale's number lower.
setup.caption: 2. Press down hard on the table. Watch the number.

setup.art: The same child gently lifting up under the table edge with fingertips, the scale's number higher.
setup.caption: 3. Gently pull up under the table edge. Watch again.

setup.art: The child bending knees quickly, the dial needle swinging.
setup.caption: 4. Bend your knees quickly. Watch the number jump.

flow.do: 1. Put the scale on a hard floor next to a strong table. 2. Your child stands still on it with both feet. 3. Read and write the number when it settles.
flow.say: Stand still on the scale. What number does it show? Let's write it down.
flow.kid: Stand still on the scale. Read the number. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bathroom scale experiment. You read the scale while standing still.
flow.parent: A child of 25 kilograms is pressing down with about 250 newtons. Help multiply by 10.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess what will happen. 2. They press down hard on the table top with both palms, still standing on the scale. 3. Read the number.
flow.say: Guess first. If you press down on the table, will the number go up, down, or stay the same? Why? Now try it.
flow.kid: Guess first, and say why. Then press down hard on the table. What does the number do?
flow.context: In this step of the bathroom scale experiment, you stand on the scale and press on a table.

check.q: You stand on a bathroom scale and press down hard on a table beside you. What happens to the number?
check.why: It goes down. The table now holds up part of you, so your feet push less on the scale. Picking 'goes up' usually means pushing hard feels like adding weight. Picking 'stays the same' usually means the scale is thought to show how much of you there is. It really shows your push.

flow.parent: Wait for the guess and the reason before your child presses. The number goes down, because the table now holds up part of your child.

flow.do: 1. Your child gently lifts up on the underside of the table edge with their fingertips. 2. Read the number. 3. Then they bend their knees quickly, once, and watch the needle or digits.
flow.say: Now gently pull up under the table edge. What do you think the number will do? Why? Try it. Then bend your knees quickly and watch.
flow.kid: Gently pull up under the table edge. Watch the number. Then bend your knees fast. Watch again.
flow.context: This step of the bathroom scale experiment tests pulling up on a table, and bending your knees fast.
flow.parent: Pulling up on the table makes the number go up, because the table pushes your child down. Bending the knees makes the number dip, then jump up as they stop. Nobody got heavier or lighter.

flow.do: Ask the big question and let your child answer before you explain.
flow.say: Did you get any heavier or lighter just now? Did any of you go away, or any more of you arrive? So what is the scale really showing?
flow.kid: Did any of you disappear? So what does the scale show? Say what you think.
flow.context: This step of the bathroom scale experiment asks what a scale really shows.

ask.q: What does the scale really show?
good: How hard I push on it.
My push, not how much of me there is.
The force of my feet on it.

flow.think: On the Moon, would the scale show a bigger number, a smaller number, or the same?
flow.parent: Let your child answer first. Then you can say it: the scale shows how hard you push on it. The amount of you never changed.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think the scale shows? Which numbers show it? And why did the number change when you pressed the table?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What the scale really shows. Which numbers show it. Why it changed.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the scale shows my push. What I saw: it showed 25 standing still, 18 pressing the table and 29 pulling up. Why: the table took some of my push, or added to it. There was always the same amount of me.
flow.context: This is the last step of the bathroom scale experiment. You explain what you found, like a scientist.

experiments.title: Can Your Hands Be Fooled? The Big Box and the Small Box
experiments.context: This is the big box and small box experiment. You make a big box and a small box pull exactly the same on a forcemeter. Then you ask people which one feels heavier.
experiments.question: If two boxes pull a forcemeter with exactly the same force, will they feel the same when we lift them?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will people say the big box feels heavier, the small box feels heavier, or that they feel the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Make both boxes pull the forcemeter to exactly the same number. Wrap them the same way, so the outside looks alike. Ask each person to lift both boxes the same way, with one hand, by the same string loop. Ask at least 5 people.
results_table: Which felt heavier: big, small or same?

materials.item: a forcemeter, 0 to 10 newtons
a small box, like a matchbox or a small tin
a big empty cardboard box, like a shoe box
coins, dal or sand to fill the small box
string and sticky tape
5 or more people to test

experiments.safety: Keep the boxes light, under 5 newtons each. Wash hands after handling coins or sand.

schedule.what: Make two boxes that pull the same on a forcemeter. Ask at least 5 people which one feels heavier.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Count how many people chose each answer. Draw a bar chart.

setup.caption: 1. Hang the big box on the forcemeter. Read its pull.
setup.art: An empty shoe box hanging from a forcemeter by a string loop, the pointer on 3 N.

setup.caption: 2. Fill the small box until it pulls exactly the same.
setup.art: A small tin hanging from the same forcemeter, coins being added, the pointer on 3 N.
A blindfolded grown-up lifting the small box in one hand and the big box in the other by their strings.
setup.caption: 3. Ask people to lift both. Which feels heavier?

flow.do: 1. Tie a string loop to the big empty box with tape. 2. Hang it on the forcemeter and read its pull. 3. Tie a loop to the small box. 4. Fill the small box with coins or dal until it pulls exactly the same number. 5. Tape it shut.
flow.say: These two boxes must pull with exactly the same force. Keep adding coins until the forcemeter shows the same number for both.
flow.kid: Hang the big box. Read the number. Fill the small box until it shows the same number. Tape it shut.
flow.context: This is the first step of the big box and small box experiment. You make two boxes that pull exactly the same.
flow.parent: An empty shoe box pulls about 2 to 3 newtons. If the big box is very light, put a little crumpled paper and a few coins inside it too. What matters is that both read the same.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess what people will say, and write the guess down.
flow.say: Both boxes pull the forcemeter the same. Will people feel that? What do you think they will say, and why?
flow.kid: Both boxes pull the same. What will people say? Why? Write your guess.
flow.context: This step of the big box and small box experiment is your guess, before you ask people.

ask.q: Why do you think people will say that?
good: Big things are usually heavier.
They pull the same, so they will feel the same.
Small things feel heavier in your hand.

flow.do: 1. Ask each person to lift both boxes, one in each hand, by the string loops. 2. Don't tell them what you did. 3. Ask: 'Which feels heavier?' 4. Write each answer in the table.
flow.say: Please lift these two boxes. Which one feels heavier to you?
flow.kid: Ask a person to lift both boxes. Ask which feels heavier. Write their answer.
flow.context: This is the main part of the big box and small box experiment. You ask at least 5 people which box feels heavier.
flow.parent: Most people say the small box feels heavier, often much heavier. Some even refuse to believe the forcemeter.

flow.do: Count the answers and draw a bar for each one.
flow.say: Let's count. How many people said small? How many said big? How many said the same?
flow.kid: Count the answers. Draw one bar for small, big and same.
flow.context: This step of the big box and small box experiment counts what people said.

chart.title: Made-up example results: which box felt heavier to 6 people?
chart.note: Both boxes pulled the forcemeter to exactly the same number. These results are made up. Yours may be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. Can our hands be fooled? Which answers show it? And why do you think people felt the small box was heavier?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think about hands. Which answers show it. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: hands can be fooled. What I saw: both boxes showed 3 newtons, but 5 of 6 people said the small one felt heavier. Why: our brains expect big things to be heavier, so the big box surprised them by being light.
flow.context: This is the last step of the big box and small box experiment. You explain what you found, like a scientist.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: which box felt heavier to 6 people?
example_chart.note: Both boxes pulled the forcemeter to exactly the same number. These results are made up. Yours may be different.

activities.title: The Squash-o-meter: how big is that push?

materials.item: a balloon, blown up to the size of a big mango
five things to push: a plastic cup, a book, a chair, a full bucket of water, the wall

activities.safety: Don't blow the balloon too full. Keep it away from sharp corners. Push the bucket gently, so water doesn't spill.

schedule.what: Push five things with a balloon and watch how much it squashes.

activities.record: Draw the balloon for each push: a little bit squashed, half squashed or very squashed. Write small, medium or large force.
activities.context: This is the balloon push activity. You push different things with a balloon instead of your hands, and watch what the balloon does.

setup.art: A child pushing a plastic cup along a table with a round balloon, the balloon barely dented.
setup.caption: 1. Push a cup with the balloon. It hardly squashes.

setup.art: The same child pushing a chair with the balloon, the balloon half flattened.
setup.caption: 2. Push a chair. The balloon squashes more.

setup.art: The child pushing the wall with the balloon, the balloon pressed flat.
setup.caption: 3. Push the wall. It squashes flat, but the wall doesn't move.

flow.do: 1. Blow up a balloon to about the size of a big mango and tie it. 2. Show your child how to hold it in both hands and push something with the balloon, not with the hands.
flow.say: Today you push things with the balloon, not with your hands. Watch the balloon each time. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Hold the balloon in both hands. Push things with the balloon. Watch it. What do you notice?
flow.context: This is the first step of the balloon push activity. You push things through a balloon and watch it.

flow.do: Your child pushes five things through the balloon. They are a plastic cup, a book, a chair, a full bucket of water and the wall. They push each one until it moves, or as hard as they can for the wall.
flow.say: Push each thing until it just starts to move. What does the balloon do? Which push squashes it most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Push the cup. Then the book, the chair, the bucket and the wall. How squashed is the balloon each time?
flow.context: This is the main part of the balloon push activity. You push five things and watch the balloon squash.

ask.q: The wall didn't move. Was there still a force?
good: Yes, the balloon squashed flat.
Yes, a big push, but the wall is too strong to move.

flow.do: Ask your child to put the five pushes in order, smallest to biggest. Then they say small, medium or large for each.
flow.say: Put the pushes in order. Which was the smallest? Which was the biggest? Could the balloon tell us an exact number? Why not?
flow.kid: Put the pushes in order, smallest first. Could a balloon tell you an exact number?
flow.context: This is the last step of the balloon push activity. You put the pushes in order and think about numbers.
flow.think: A balloon shows big and small, but not an exact number. What tool could give us a number?

activities.title: Feel One Newton

materials.item: sealed 100 gram packets, like tea, biscuits or salt (look for 100 g printed on the packet)
a 1 litre bottle of water
a 1 kilogram packet of atta, rice or salt
a small apple

activities.safety: Hold the heavier things low over a bed or a cushion, in case they slip.

schedule.what: Hold 1, 5 and 10 newtons. Make a one newton kit.

activities.record: Draw your one newton kit. Write '1 N' beside each thing that pulls with about 1 newton.
activities.context: This is the one newton activity. You hold things that pull with 1 newton and 10 newtons. Your hands learn the size of a newton.

setup.art: A child's open palm holding a 100 gram tea packet, labelled 1 N.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a 100 gram packet. That is about 1 newton.

setup.art: A child holding a 1 litre water bottle in one hand, labelled 10 N.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a 1 litre bottle of water. That is about 10 newtons.

setup.art: A tray with an apple, a tea packet, a banana and a small steel bowl, labelled 'My 1 newton kit'.
setup.caption: 3. Find other things that feel like 1 newton.

flow.do: 1. Put one 100 gram packet on your child's open palm. 2. Say that it pulls down with about 1 newton. 3. Then put a small apple on the other palm.
flow.say: Hold this packet on your open hand. It has 100 grams of tea in it. Scientists say it pulls down with about 1 newton. Now hold the apple. Does it pull more, less or the same?
flow.kid: Hold the packet on your open hand. Feel it pull down. That is about 1 newton.
flow.context: This is the first step of the one newton activity. You feel what 1 newton is like.

flow.do: 1. Give your child a 1 litre bottle of water. 2. Say it pulls with about 10 newtons. 3. Then let them hold the 1 kilogram atta packet. 4. Ask how many 100 gram packets would make the same pull.
flow.say: This bottle pulls with about 10 newtons. How many tea packets do you think would pull as hard as this bottle? Why?
flow.kid: Hold the water bottle. It pulls about 10 newtons. How many tea packets would match it?
flow.context: This step of the one newton activity compares 1 newton with 10 newtons.

ask.q: How many 100 gram packets make 10 newtons?
good: 10 packets, because each one is about 1 newton.
10, because 10 times 100 grams is 1 kilogram.

flow.parent: A 1 litre bottle holds about 1 kilogram of water. On Earth, each kilogram pulls with about 10 newtons. More exactly, it is 9.8 newtons, but 10 is close enough for us.

flow.do: Your child walks around the kitchen and finds three other things that feel like about 1 newton. They check each one on a kitchen scale or its packet label: about 100 grams.
flow.say: Find three more things that feel like about 1 newton. Then let's check them on the scale or the label.
flow.kid: Find three things that feel like 1 newton. Check them. Are they about 100 grams?
flow.context: This is the last step of the one newton activity. You make your own one newton kit.
flow.think: A small apple is about 1 newton on Earth. Would it still be 1 newton on the Moon?

activities.title: Read It Right: the forcemeter drill

materials.item: the printed paper forcemeter scale, 0 to 10 newtons, with half-newton marks
a strip of card with a red line on it, for the pointer
scissors and sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Make a paper forcemeter and practise reading 8 settings.

activities.record: Write each reading with its unit, for example '3 and a half newtons'.
activities.context: This is the forcemeter reading practice. You make a paper forcemeter with a sliding pointer, and practise reading it at eye level.

setup.art: A long paper strip with numbers 0 to 10 and small marks between them, a card slider with a red line clipped over it.
setup.caption: 1. Make the paper forcemeter and its sliding pointer.

setup.art: A grown-up sliding the pointer to a number while the child looks with eyes level with the pointer.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up sets the pointer. You read it at eye level.

setup.art: A child's eye above the scale, a dotted line showing a slanted view, and a red cross.
setup.caption: 3. Try reading from above. See how it can trick you.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the paper scale and the card pointer. 2. Fold the pointer card around the scale so it can slide up and down.
flow.say: We're going to make a pretend forcemeter. The pointer slides, just like the real one.
flow.kid: Cut out the scale and the pointer. Fold the pointer round the scale. Slide it up and down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the forcemeter reading practice. You make a paper forcemeter.

flow.do: 1. Slide the pointer to a reading, without your child seeing. 2. They read it, with their eyes level with the pointer. 3. Do 8 readings: 2, 5, 7 and a half, 0, 3 and a half, 9, 1 and a half, 10.
flow.say: Count the big numbers first. Then count the little marks after it. Each little mark is half a newton.
flow.kid: Read the big number first. Then count the small marks. Each one is half a newton. Say the unit too.
flow.context: This is the main part of the forcemeter reading practice. A grown-up sets the pointer and you read it.

chart.title: Practice reading. Each small mark is half a newton.
chart.label: What does this forcemeter read?

check.q: The pointer is on the small mark halfway between 7 and 8. Each small mark is half a newton. What is the reading?
check.why: 7 and a half newtons. The pointer is past 7 by one small mark, and each small mark is half a newton. Picking 7 or 8 usually means the small marks were not counted. Picking 75 usually means the 7 and the 5 of 'point 5' were read as one number.

flow.do: Let your child look at the pointer from high above, then from below, then level. Ask which one looks right.
flow.say: Look from up high. Now from down low. Now straight on. Does the number seem to change? Which one do you trust? Why?
flow.kid: Look from high up. Then from low down. Then straight on. Which way is true?
flow.context: This is the last step of the forcemeter reading practice. You see why we read at eye level.
flow.think: Why do you think scientists always say 'eye level'?

activities.title: Tug of War on Two Forcemeters

materials.item: two forcemeters of the same range, 0 to 10 or 0 to 50 newtons
a second person

activities.safety: Pull gently and slowly. Never let go suddenly while the springs are stretched. Stay below the biggest number on the scale.

schedule.what: Hook two forcemeters together and pull. Compare the two readings.

activities.record: Write both readings for 4 different tugs. Draw an arrow on each side.
activities.context: This is the forcemeter tug of war. Two people hook two forcemeters together and pull. You compare the two readings.

setup.art: Two forcemeters hooked hook-to-hook, a child holding one end and a grown-up holding the other.
setup.caption: 1. Hook the two forcemeters together.

setup.art: The child and grown-up pulling gently, both pointers on 5 N.
setup.caption: 2. Pull gently. Read both forcemeters.

setup.art: The child holding one forcemeter, the other one's ring hooked over a door handle, both reading 4 N.
setup.caption: 3. Hook one to a door handle. Pull again.

flow.do: 1. Check both forcemeters read zero. 2. Hook them together, hook to hook. 3. Each person holds one by its top ring.
flow.say: Two forcemeters, hooked together. When we pull, will both show the same number, or will the stronger person's show more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hook the two forcemeters together. Hold yours. Will both show the same number? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the forcemeter tug of war. You hook two forcemeters together and guess what they will show.
flow.parent: Most children guess that the grown-up's forcemeter will show more. Wait for the guess and the reason before anyone pulls.

flow.do: 1. Pull gently, the grown-up harder than the child. 2. Hold still and read both. 3. Try 4 different tugs. 4. Write both readings each time.
flow.say: I'll pull harder. Now read both forcemeters. What do you see?
flow.kid: Pull gently. Hold still. Read both numbers. Are they the same?
flow.context: This is the main part of the forcemeter tug of war. You pull and read both forcemeters each time.

ask.q: Why do both forcemeters always show the same number?
good: Each one pulls on the other.
When I pull it, it pulls me back just as hard.
The pull goes through both springs.

flow.do: Hook one forcemeter to a door handle by its ring. Your child pulls on the other one. Read both.
flow.say: Now the door is my partner. Pull. Does the door's forcemeter show the same number as yours?
flow.kid: Hook one to a door handle. Pull the other. Is the door pulling back?
flow.context: This is the last step of the forcemeter tug of war. You see that even a door pulls back.
flow.think: If you pull on the door with 5 newtons, how hard is the door pulling you?
flow.parent: The door pulls back with exactly the same force. Every pull comes with an equal pull back. Isaac Newton wrote this as his third law of motion. The unit on Pushes and pulls explores it more.

activities.title: Your Tiffin on the Moon

materials.item: a tiffin box
600 grams of uncooked rice
a kitchen scale
a forcemeter, if you have one
a bowl

activities.safety: Do it over a tray, so spilled rice is easy to pick up.

schedule.what: Feel your lunch's pull on Earth, the Moon and Jupiter.

activities.record: Write the pull on Earth, the Moon and Jupiter. Draw the three tiffins.
activities.context: This is the Moon tiffin activity. You change the rice in a tiffin box. Your hand feels how hard your lunch would pull on the Moon and on Jupiter.

setup.art: A tiffin box of rice on a kitchen scale reading 600 g.
setup.caption: 1. Fill a tiffin with 600 grams of rice. That pulls about 6 newtons on Earth.

setup.art: Rice being poured out of the tiffin into a bowl until the scale shows 100 g, a little Moon drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Pour out rice until 100 grams are left. That is the Moon's pull.

setup.art: A bag of rice on the scale reading 1,500 g, a striped Jupiter drawn beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Now fill a bag with 1,500 grams. That is about Jupiter's pull.

flow.do: 1. Weigh 600 grams of rice into the tiffin. 2. Your child holds it. 3. Say that on Earth it pulls with about 6 newtons.
flow.say: Hold your lunch. On Earth it pulls your hand down with about 6 newtons. The Moon pulls things down about one sixth as hard. How do you think your lunch would feel there? Why?
flow.kid: Hold the tiffin. It pulls about 6 newtons here on Earth. The Moon pulls six times less. How would it feel there?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Moon tiffin activity. You feel your lunch's pull on Earth.

flow.do: 1. Ask: 'What is one sixth of 600 grams?' 2. Pour rice out until the scale shows 100 grams. 3. Your child holds it. 4. Say that this is how your full tiffin would feel on the Moon.
flow.say: On the Moon, your full tiffin would pull like this. Feel it. But how much rice would really be inside the tiffin on the Moon?
flow.kid: Pour out rice until 100 grams are left. That is your full lunch on the Moon. Feel how light!
flow.context: This step of the Moon tiffin activity shows how your lunch would feel on the Moon.

ask.q: On the Moon, would there be less rice in your tiffin?
good: No, the same rice. The Moon just pulls it less.
The mass is the same. Only the weight is smaller.

flow.do: 1. Fill a bag with 1,500 grams of rice. 2. Your child holds it. 3. Say this is how the same 600 gram tiffin would feel on Jupiter, about two and a half times heavier.
flow.say: Jupiter is a giant planet. Its pull is about two and a half times stronger than Earth's. This is how your lunch would feel there.
flow.kid: Hold this bag. It is your lunch on Jupiter. Two and a half times heavier!
flow.context: This is the last step of the Moon tiffin activity. You feel how your lunch would pull on Jupiter.
flow.think: Your lunch felt different in three places. Did your lunch change, or did the planet change?

chart.title: How hard the same 600 gram tiffin pulls down in three places

activities.title: Who Checks the Scales? A market visit

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a grown-up to go with you

activities.safety: Go with a grown-up. Be polite, and ask before touching any scale.

schedule.what: Visit a market. Find different scales and their seals. Ask the shopkeeper questions.

activities.record: Draw three different scales you saw. Write what each one weighs or shows, and whether you found a seal.
activities.context: This is a visit to a market or shop. You look at shop scales and find the seals that show they were checked. Then you ask how the shopkeeper keeps weighing fair.

setup.art: A busy vegetable market with a digital scale, a hanging spring balance and a two-pan balance on three stalls.
setup.caption: 1. Find three different kinds of scale.

setup.art: A close-up of a small lead seal or sticker stamp on the side of a shop scale.
setup.caption: 2. Look for the checking seal or stamp.

setup.art: A child asking a smiling shopkeeper a question, notebook in hand.
setup.caption: 3. Ask the shopkeeper how they keep their scale fair.

flow.do: 1. Walk through a vegetable market or visit a kirana shop. 2. Help your child find different kinds of scales: digital, hanging spring balances and two-pan balances.
flow.say: Let's count the scales. How many kinds can we find? Which ones use a spring? Which ones compare with iron weights?
flow.kid: Look for scales. Count how many kinds. Which ones have a spring? Which have two pans?
flow.context: This is the first step of the market visit. You look for different kinds of scales.

flow.do: Look closely at a scale with your child and find the seal or stamp of the Legal Metrology department. Ask the shopkeeper's permission first.
flow.say: This little seal means a government officer tested this scale with standard weights. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: Look for a little seal or stamp on the scale. It shows someone checked it.
flow.context: This step of the market visit looks for the seal that shows a scale was checked.
flow.parent: Legal Metrology officers test shop scales with standard weights and seal the honest ones. Scales are meant to be checked regularly. If you can't find a seal, that is fine. Talk about why checking matters.

flow.do: Help your child ask the shopkeeper two questions. 'How do you know your scale is right?' 'Has anyone checked it?'
flow.say: Let's ask the shopkeeper how they know their scale is right.
flow.kid: Ask the shopkeeper: how do you know your scale is right?
flow.context: This is the last step of the market visit. You ask a shopkeeper how they keep their scale fair.
flow.think: Why might a shopkeeper want an honest scale, even if nobody checks?

activities.title: Swap Coins for Water: a unit anyone can share

materials.item: the notebook, string and cup from the coin-pull investigation
a medicine cup or a measuring jug with millilitre marks
a jug of water
a tray or a towel under the cup

activities.safety: Put a tray or towel under the cup, and wipe up spills straight away, so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Start the notebook sliding with water instead of coins. Turn the millilitres into newtons.

activities.record: Write how many millilitres of water started the notebook sliding. Divide by 100 to get newtons. Write it next to your coin number.
activities.context: This is the water-pull activity. It follows the coin-pull investigation. You start the same notebook sliding with water instead of coins. Water is the same everywhere, so anyone can repeat your test, and your answer turns into newtons.

setup.art: The same notebook, string and hanging cup as in the coin test, with a child pouring water into the cup from a small medicine cup marked in millilitres.
setup.caption: 1. Pour water into the hanging cup, 10 millilitres at a time.

setup.art: The notebook starting to slide, water sloshing in the cup above a towel, and a tally of 10s written on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Stop when the notebook slides. Add up the millilitres.

setup.art: A small glass of 100 millilitres of water and a small apple side by side on a balance, level, labelled 'about 1 newton each'.
setup.caption: 3. Every 100 millilitres of water pulls with about 1 newton.

flow.do: 1. Empty the coins out of the cup and hang it again. 2. Ask your child to guess how much water will start the notebook sliding, and why.
flow.say: Your cousin can't use our coins. But she has water. How much water do you think it will take to slide one notebook? Why?
flow.kid: Now you will use water, not coins. How much water will start the notebook sliding? Guess, and say why.

ask.q: How did you make your guess?
good: I thought about how heavy the coins felt.
The cup was nearly full of coins, so maybe half a cup of water.
Water is lighter than coins, so more of it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the water-pull activity. You guess how much water will do the job of your coins.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into the hanging cup 10 millilitres at a time. 2. Make a mark on paper for each 10 millilitres. 3. Stop when the notebook starts to slide. 4. Add up the millilitres. 5. Do it 2 more times and use the middle number.
flow.say: Ten millilitres at a time. Mark each one. Stop when it slides.
flow.kid: Pour in 10 millilitres. Make a mark. Pour again. Stop when the notebook slides. Add up your marks.
flow.parent: One thin notebook often needs between 30 and 60 millilitres. Pour slowly near the end. If it needs more than the cup holds, use a bigger paper cup.
flow.context: This is the main part of the water-pull activity. You pour water into the cup until the notebook slides.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that 100 millilitres of water pulls down with about 1 newton, anywhere on Earth. 2. Ask them to turn their millilitres into newtons.
flow.say: Here is a fact people everywhere share: 100 millilitres of water pulls down with about 1 newton. So how many newtons did our notebook need?
flow.kid: 100 millilitres of water pulls with about 1 newton. How many newtons did your notebook need?

check.q: In the water-pull test, the notebook slid when the cup held 50 millilitres of water. 100 millilitres pulls with about 1 newton. How big was the pull?
check.why: 50 millilitres is half of 100 millilitres, so it pulls with about half of 1 newton. Picking 50 newtons uses the millilitres as if they were newtons. A number needs the right unit. Picking 5 newtons usually means dividing by 10 instead of by 100.

flow.parent: 100 millilitres of water is 100 grams, and the Earth pulls 100 grams down with just under 1 newton. The cup and string add a tiny pull too. It is small, so we leave it out.
flow.context: This step of the water-pull activity turns your water into newtons, the unit everyone shares.

flow.do: Ask why water might be a better unit than coins. Let your child answer first.
flow.say: Could your cousin in another city repeat this test exactly? Why might water be a better unit than our coins?
flow.kid: Could your cousin repeat this test? Why is water better than your coins?

ask.q: Why is water a good thing to share?
good: Water is the same everywhere.
Anyone can get water and fill a 100 millilitre cup.
Coins are different in different countries.

flow.parent: France first defined the gram in 1795 in almost this way. It was the mass of a little cube of water, 1 centimetre on each side. Today the kilogram is fixed by a number from nature instead.
flow.think: Water changes a tiny bit when it is hot or cold. Would a perfect unit need something that never changes at all?
flow.context: This is the last step of the water-pull activity. You think about why water makes a unit anyone can share.

projects.title: Build Your Own Forcemeter
projects.context: This is the forcemeter building project. You make a forcemeter from a rubber band, a paper clip and a strip of card. You mark its scale using 100 gram packets, and then test it against a kitchen scale.

materials.item: a strong rubber band
a 30 cm strip of stiff card, or a 30 cm ruler
a paper clip, opened into an S-shaped hook
a small polythene bag with handles
five sealed 100 gram packets of salt, dal or tea
a drawing pin, sticky tape and a marker pen
a kitchen scale, if you have one

projects.safety: A grown-up pushes in the drawing pin. Don't stretch the rubber band near anyone's face. If it is stretched thin and white, it may snap, so stop adding packets.

schedule.what: Build the forcemeter. Mark the scale from 0 to 5 newtons with 100 gram packets.
Test five things with your forcemeter. Check them with a kitchen scale or a real forcemeter. Improve your forcemeter.

projects.record: Draw your forcemeter and label the band, the hook, the bag and the scale. Write a table: Thing, My forcemeter (N), Check (N).

setup.art: A card strip taped upright to a table leg, a rubber band hanging from a drawing pin at the top, an S-hook made from a paper clip at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a rubber band from the top of a card strip. Add a paper clip hook.

setup.art: A small polythene bag hanging from the hook, a child drawing a line labelled 0 at the bottom of the band.
setup.caption: 2. Hang the empty bag. Mark '0' where the band ends.

setup.art: One 100 gram packet in the bag, the band longer, a new line labelled 1 N.
setup.caption: 3. Add one 100 gram packet. Mark '1 N'.

setup.art: Five packets in the bag, marks from 0 to 5 N on the card.
setup.caption: 4. Keep adding packets. Mark 2 N, 3 N, 4 N and 5 N.

flow.do: 1. Tape the card strip upright to a table leg or a door frame. 2. A grown-up pushes the drawing pin into the top. 3. Hang the rubber band from the pin. 4. Open a paper clip into an S-shape and hang it from the band.
flow.say: We're going to build a real forcemeter. The rubber band will be our spring.
flow.kid: Tape the card upright. Hang the rubber band from the pin. Hook a bent paper clip on the bottom.
flow.context: This is the first step of the forcemeter building project. You put the parts together.

flow.do: 1. Hang the empty bag on the paper clip. 2. Your child draws a line on the card exactly where the bottom of the band is. 3. They write 0 beside it.
flow.say: The empty bag is our starting point. Draw a line where the bottom of the band is. That is our zero.
flow.kid: Hang the empty bag. Draw a line where the band ends. Write 0.
flow.context: This step of the forcemeter building project marks the zero.

flow.do: 1. Put one 100 gram packet in the bag. 2. Wait for it to stop bouncing. 3. Mark the new place '1 N'. 4. Add packets one at a time and mark 2 N, 3 N, 4 N and 5 N.
flow.say: Each 100 gram packet pulls with about 1 newton. Before we add the second packet, guess: will it stretch the band the same amount as the first? Why? Let's mark each one.
flow.kid: Add one packet. Wait till it stops bouncing. Mark 1 N. Keep going to 5 N.
flow.context: This is the main part of day 1 of the forcemeter building project. You mark the scale with 100 gram packets. Scientists call this calibrating.

ask.q: Are the gaps between your marks the same size?
good: Almost the same.
They get a bit bigger, or a bit smaller, as the band stretches more.

flow.parent: With a rubber band, the gaps are often not quite equal. A metal spring gives much more even gaps. The unit on Stretching and springs explores why. That is one reason real forcemeters use metal springs.

flow.do: Take all the packets out. Check whether the band goes back to the 0 line.
flow.say: Does the band go back to zero when we take everything out?
flow.kid: Take the packets out. Does the band go back to 0?
flow.context: This is the last step of day 1 of the forcemeter building project. You check whether the band springs back to zero.
flow.think: What would happen to your marks if the band got tired and stayed a little stretched?

flow.do: Day 2. 1. Check the zero again. 2. Hang five things in the bag, one at a time. Try an apple, a steel spoon, a pencil box, a small water bottle and a potato. 3. Write each reading. 4. Check each one on a kitchen scale and divide the grams by 100, or use a real forcemeter.
flow.say: Before we check, guess: will our forcemeter agree with the kitchen scale? Why? Now let's see if it tells the truth.
flow.kid: Check the zero. Hang five things. Write the newtons. Then check them on the kitchen scale. Do they agree?
flow.context: This is day 2 of the forcemeter building project. You test your forcemeter against a kitchen scale.
flow.wait: Do this step on the next day.

chart.title: Made-up example: checking the homemade forcemeter

flow.do: Ask your child what they could change to make their forcemeter better, and let them try one change.
flow.say: Real scientists always improve their tools. What could make ours better? Why do you think that would help?
flow.kid: How could you make your forcemeter better? Try one idea.
flow.context: This is the last step of the forcemeter building project. You improve your forcemeter, like a real engineer.
flow.parent: Two bands side by side stretch less, so the forcemeter can show bigger pulls. A thin band stretches more, so it can show smaller pulls more clearly.

challenges.title: Catch a Feather's Pull
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. Most forcemeters can't show the pull of a sheet of paper, because its pull is far smaller than 1 newton. Your job is to design a tool that can show it.
challenges.problem: A sheet of paper pulls down with only about one twentieth of a newton. A normal forcemeter doesn't even move. Design a tool that shows a clear difference between one sheet of paper and two sheets.
constraints: Use only things you can find at home.
Your tool must show the difference between 1 sheet and 2 sheets clearly.
You must be able to repeat it and get the same result.
materials: thin rubber bands or hair elastics
thread, sticky tape and paper clips
general: Use a very thin rubber band. A thinner band stretches more for the same pull.
Use a long plastic ruler. Tape one end to the edge of a table so it sticks out. Hang the paper from the far end. Use a second ruler to see how far the end bends down.
Make a balance. Put a straw on a pin through its middle, and hang paper on one end.
creative: Tape a long straw to the end of the bending ruler as a pointer. A small bend at the ruler becomes a bigger movement at the tip.
Henry Cavendish measured a force about as big as a sand grain's weight, with a twisting wire. Can you use a twisting thread?
Scientists feel the push of single atoms with a tiny bending needle. Your bending ruler is a giant model of it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own tiny-force meter. Draw it, build it, and test it with 1, 2 and 3 sheets of paper. Can it tell them apart every time?

setup.art: A plastic ruler taped to the edge of a table, sticking out, a folded sheet of paper hanging from its free end on a thread.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a ruler to the table edge so it sticks out. Hang paper from the end.

setup.art: A second ruler standing upright beside the free end, showing how far it bends down.
setup.caption: 2. Use a second ruler to see how far the end bends down.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper hanging from the ruler, bending it further, the upright ruler showing the difference.
setup.caption: 3. Add a second sheet. Does the bend get bigger?

flow.do: Read the problem with your child. Hang a sheet of paper on a normal forcemeter and show that the pointer barely moves.
flow.say: Look. The forcemeter doesn't even notice the paper. We need a much more sensitive tool. What do you think makes a tool more sensitive?
flow.kid: Hang paper on the forcemeter. The pointer hardly moves! You need a better tool.
flow.context: This is the first step of the feather's pull challenge. You see why a normal forcemeter can't show the pull of paper.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions together. Then read the creative ideas.
flow.say: Here are some ways people usually do it. And here are some cleverer ideas. Which do you want to try?
flow.kid: Read the ideas. Pick one to try, or invent your own.
flow.context: This step of the feather's pull challenge looks at ideas for a very sensitive tool.

flow.do: Help your child build their chosen tool. Test it with 1, 2 and 3 sheets of paper. Write down the stretch or bend each time.
flow.say: Build it, then test it. Does it show 1 sheet, 2 sheets and 3 sheets clearly? Try each one twice.
flow.kid: Build your tool. Test it with 1, 2 and 3 sheets. Write down how far it moves each time.
flow.context: This is the main part of the feather's pull challenge. You build your tiny-force meter and test it.
flow.parent: With a 30 cm plastic ruler sticking out about 25 cm, one sheet usually bends it a few millimetres. A straw pointer makes it easier to see.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain why their tool works, and how they could make it even more sensitive.
flow.say: Why does your tool notice paper when the forcemeter doesn't?
flow.kid: Why does your tool work? How could it notice even smaller pulls?
flow.context: This is the last step of the feather's pull challenge. You explain why your tool works.
flow.think: Could you make a tool that shows the pull of one hair? What would you change?

challenges.title: A Fair Check for Every Scale
challenges.context: This is a fairness challenge. A village has no shop that sells standard weights. Your job is to design a way for anyone to check whether a scale is honest. You may use only water and things at home.
challenges.problem: A village market has five scales, and people think some are wrong. There are no standard iron weights. Design a fair way for anyone to check every scale, using water.
constraints: You may use water, bottles, a measuring jug and things from the kitchen.
Your check must work for both small and big readings.
Anyone in the village, even a child, must be able to do your check.
materials: a measuring jug with millilitre marks
empty plastic bottles of 500 millilitres and 1 litre
a kitchen scale, a hanging spring balance or a forcemeter to check
general: Fill a bottle with exactly 1 litre of water. That is 1 kilogram of water, plus the bottle, and pulls with about 10 newtons.
First check the zero. Then check the scale with 1 litre, then 2 litres.
Write the results on a chart and stick it near the scale.
creative: The gram was first defined, in 1795, as the mass of one cubic centimetre of water. That is one millilitre. So water was the first standard for the gram. You are doing what the inventors of the gram did.
Weigh the empty bottle first, and take it away from every reading. That makes your check more exact.
Make a check-kit: one 100 millilitre bottle, one 500 millilitre bottle and one 1 litre bottle, each sealed and labelled.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own check-kit. Test it on your kitchen scale or forcemeter. Write instructions simple enough for a 6-year-old to follow.

setup.art: A measuring jug pouring water into a 1 litre bottle up to a marked line.
setup.caption: 1. Pour exactly 1 litre of water into a bottle.

setup.art: The bottle on a kitchen scale showing just over 1,000 grams.
setup.caption: 2. Put the bottle on the scale. It should show just over 1,000 grams.

setup.art: A row of three sealed labelled bottles: 100 ml, 500 ml and 1 litre, labelled 'Check kit'.
setup.caption: 3. Make a check-kit of bottles for small and big readings.

flow.do: Read the problem with your child. Talk about the story of Pushpa, who checked a spring balance with packets of salt, if you have read it.
flow.say: Imagine there are no salt packets and no iron weights. What could we use that always weighs the same, and that everybody trusts?
flow.kid: No standard weights. What could you use instead? What weighs the same every time?
flow.context: This is the first step of the fair scale challenge. You think about what everybody could trust.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together.
flow.say: Here is one idea people have used: one litre of water always has a mass of about 1 kilogram. Why do you think water could work as a check that everybody shares?
flow.kid: Read the ideas. Water can be your standard. One litre is about 1 kilogram.
flow.context: This step of the fair scale challenge looks at how water can be a standard weight.

worksheets.title: How Big Is a Pull? (core)

items.p: In the coin-pull test, coins in a cup pulled a notebook until it slid. Why did you use coins of only one kind?
opts: Every coin of one kind pulls the same amount, so each one is the same unit
It makes the notebook slide faster
items.why: A unit must be the same every time. One kind of coin gives the same small pull again and again. Picking 'mixed coins are heavier' misses the point. Mixed coins pull by different amounts, so a count of them means nothing.

items.p: In the coin-pull test, Ravi needed 6 big coins to slide a notebook. His mother needed 12 small coins for the same notebook. Who found the bigger pull?
opts: Neither. It was the same pull, counted in different units
items.why: Same notebook, same table, so the same pull. The small coins were lighter, so more of them were needed. Picking 'his mother' means trusting the number 12 without its unit.

items.p: In the coin-pull test, two stacked notebooks usually need about twice as many coins as one notebook.
items.why: True. The stack presses down on the table about twice as hard, so it grips about twice as much. Real results are never perfectly even, so 'about twice' is right.

items.p: What unit do scientists everywhere use for force?
items.why: Scientists everywhere count force in newtons. Picking centimetres or litres usually means force is mixed up with length or amount of water. Picking forcemeters mixes up the tool with the unit. The forcemeter is the tool. The newton is the unit.

items.p: Which tool shows the size of a pull in newtons?
items.why: A forcemeter shows pulls. A ruler shows length, a thermometer shows how hot something is, and a clock shows time.

items.p: The short way to write newtons is ____.
items.why: N stands for newton, named after Isaac Newton.

items.p: Put these in order from the smallest force to the biggest: a bird picking up a leaf, a train pulling wagons, a girl lifting a book, a horse pulling a cart. Which comes first?
items.why: The bird picking up a leaf uses the smallest force. The order is bird, girl, horse, train. Picking the train usually means the order was read from biggest to smallest.

items.p: What does the pointer of this forcemeter show?
items.why: The pointer is one small mark past 4, and each small mark is half a newton. So the reading is 4 and a half newtons. Picking 4 or 5 usually means the small marks were not counted.

chart.title: A forcemeter. Each small mark is half a newton.

items.p: Before you use a forcemeter, what should you check first?
opts: That the pointer is on zero with nothing on the hook
That the spring is very stretched
That it is the biggest forcemeter in the house
items.why: Check the zero first. If the pointer starts in the wrong place, every reading will be wrong by the same amount. Picking 'the spring is stretched' would mean it is already spoiled.

items.p: A small apple pulls down on your hand with about 1 newton.
items.why: True. A small apple of about 100 grams pulls down with about 1 newton.

items.p: If something doesn't move, no force is acting on it.
items.why: False. Push a wall with a balloon. The wall doesn't move, but the balloon squashes, so there is a big force. Forces can act on things that stay still.

items.p: Inside a forcemeter there is a ____ that stretches when you pull.
items.why: A forcemeter has a spring inside. The harder the pull, the more it stretches.

items.p: Match each tool to what it tells you.
items.why: Every measuring tool has its own job and its own unit.

items.p: Sort these into small forces and big forces.
items.why: Small forces move light things a little. Big forces move heavy things, or move things fast.

items.p: You pushed a balloon against a cup, a chair and a wall. When was the balloon most squashed?
opts: It was the same every time
items.why: The wall needed the biggest push, so the balloon squashed most, even though the wall didn't move. Picking the cup usually means a moving thing is thought to need more force.

items.p: A 1 litre bottle of water pulls down with about…
items.why: 1 litre of water has a mass of about 1 kilogram. On Earth, each kilogram pulls down with about 10 newtons. Picking 1 newton mixes the bottle up with the apple.

items.p: Why is a forcemeter better than lifting something and guessing?
items.a: My hands can be fooled. Tired arms make things feel heavier, and small heavy things feel heavier than big things that weigh the same. A forcemeter gives the same number every time.
items.why: A good answer says that feelings change, but a spring stretches the same way for the same pull.

items.p: Draw a forcemeter. Label the spring, the hook, the pointer and the scale.
items.a: The drawing shows a spring inside a tube, with a hook at the bottom. A pointer is fixed to the spring, with a scale of numbers beside it.
items.why: These four parts work together. The pull on the hook stretches the spring, and the pointer moves along the scale.

items.p: Why should you pull a forcemeter slowly and steadily?
opts: Because a jerk makes the pointer jump too high
Because forcemeters are scared of speed
items.why: A sudden jerk makes the pointer jump past the real reading for a moment. Pulling steadily gives a fair, true reading.

worksheets.title: Read It, Check It (stretch)

items.p: Your cousin did the coin-pull test with buttons and needed 11. You needed 6 coins. Can you say whose notebook needed the bigger pull? What would you need to find out?
items.a: Not yet. I would need to know how many of her buttons pull as hard as one of my coins. Or we could both use the same unit, like 100 millilitres of water or a newton.
items.why: Two numbers can only be compared in the same unit. A good answer says what to find out, not just 'yes' or 'no'.

items.p: A forcemeter shows 2 newtons with nothing on the hook. Then you hang a bag and it shows 7 newtons. How hard is the bag really pulling?
items.why: The pointer started 2 newtons too far down. So take 2 away: 7 take away 2 is 5 newtons. Picking 7 means the zero was not checked. Picking 9 means the 2 was added instead of taken away.

items.p: Which forcemeter would you choose for an apple?
opts: Neither, an apple's pull can't be shown
items.why: An apple pulls with about 1 newton. On a 0 to 10 newton forcemeter, that is easy to see. On a 0 to 1,000 newton one, the pointer would hardly move. Choose a range that fits the force.

items.p: What does this forcemeter read?
items.why: The pointer is halfway between 2 and 3, on the small mark. Each small mark is half a newton. So it reads 2 and a half newtons.

chart.title: A forcemeter. Each small mark is half a newton.

items.p: On this forcemeter, the big numbers go up in tens, and there are 10 small marks between each big number. What does each small mark stand for?
items.why: 10 newtons shared between 10 small gaps is 1 newton for each gap. Picking 10 newtons usually means the big numbers and the small marks were mixed up.

chart.title: A 0 to 100 newton forcemeter. The big numbers go up in tens.

items.p: A 1 kilogram bag of rice would show a smaller number on a forcemeter on the Moon than on Earth.
items.why: True. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard, so the forcemeter shows about 1.6 newtons instead of about 10. The rice is still the same rice.

items.p: On the Moon, what happens to a bag of rice?
opts: It has less rice in it
It has the same rice, but it pulls down less
items.why: The amount of rice, its mass, stays the same. Only the Moon's pull, its weight, is smaller. Picking 'less rice' usually means weight and mass are mixed up. Picking 'floats away' usually means the Moon is thought to have no gravity. It does, but less.

items.p: You stand on a bathroom scale and quickly bend your knees. What happens to the number?
opts: It dips and then jumps up
It goes to zero and stays there
items.why: As you drop, your feet push less, so the number dips. As you stop, they push more, so it jumps up. Nobody got heavier or lighter. The scale shows your push.

items.p: You stand on a bathroom scale and pull up gently on the underside of a table. What happens?
items.why: When you pull up on the table, the table pulls you down. So your feet push harder on the scale. Picking 'goes down' usually means pulling up is thought to lift you off the scale.

items.p: When you hook two forcemeters together and pull, both show the ____ number.
items.why: Each forcemeter pulls on the other one just as hard. Every pull comes with an equal pull back.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest force to the biggest: a grown-up standing on the floor, a sheet of paper on your hand, a crocodile's bite, a 1 litre water bottle.
items: a sheet of paper on your hand
a grown-up standing on the floor
items.why: Paper is about one twentieth of a newton. The bottle is about 10. A grown-up is about 600. A big crocodile's bite is about 16,000 newtons.

items.p: In the big box and small box experiment, both boxes pulled the forcemeter to the same number. Most people said the small box felt heavier. What does this tell us about our hands?
items.a: Our hands can be fooled. Our brains expect a big box to be heavy. When it isn't, it feels surprisingly light. So we need tools to check fairly.
items.why: This is called the size-weight illusion. A French doctor wrote about it in 1891.

items.p: Match each force to its rough size.
pairs: A small apple on your hand
A small car on the road
items.why: Every 100 grams pulls down with about 1 newton. A 25 kilogram child is about 250 newtons. A 1,000 kilogram car is about 10,000 newtons.

items.p: When you made your rubber band forcemeter, you hung 100 gram packets to put on the marks. Why did you use packets whose weight you already knew?
items.a: So that each mark would be right. A 100 gram packet pulls with about 1 newton, so I knew exactly where 1 newton was. Then 2 packets showed 2 newtons.
items.why: Putting marks on a tool using things you already know is called calibrating.

items.p: Two forcemeters were hooked together. The grown-up pulled harder, so the grown-up's forcemeter showed a bigger number.
items.why: False. Both forcemeters always show the same number. When one pulls, the other pulls back just as hard.

items.p: Draw a bathroom scale with a child standing on it. Draw an arrow for the child's push on the scale, and an arrow for the scale's push on the child.
items.a: One arrow points down from the feet onto the scale. Another arrow, the same length, points up from the scale into the feet.
items.why: The child pushes down, and the scale pushes up just as hard. That push is what the scale shows.

worksheets.title: From Molecules to the Moon (challenge)

items.p: Before 2019, the kilogram was simply whatever one metal cylinder near Paris weighed. If a speck of dust had landed on it, what would have happened to the kilogram?
items.a: By the rule of that time, the cylinder was still exactly 1 kilogram. So in a strange way, every other kilogram in the world would have become a tiny bit too small.
items.why: When a unit is one object, any change to the object changes the unit itself. That is why the kilogram is now fixed by a number from nature, the Planck constant.

items.p: One newton is defined as the push that makes a 1 kilogram thing speed up by 1 metre per second, every second. What does this tell us a force does?
opts: It only works on round things
items.why: Newton showed that a force is what changes movement. The bigger the force on the same thing, the faster it speeds up.

items.p: Inside your cells, a kinesin molecule pulls with about 6 piconewtons. That is about 6 millionths of a millionth of a newton. Which tool did scientists use to find it?
opts: Optical tweezers, made of laser light
items.why: Optical tweezers use a focused laser beam to hold a tiny bead and feel the pull on it. Arthur Ashkin invented them, and won a Nobel Prize in 2018. Ordinary scales can't feel such tiny forces.

items.p: Henry Cavendish measured the gravity pull between lead balls in 1798. What did he use to show the tiny force?
items.why: The small balls hung on a rod from a thin wire. The pull of the big balls twisted the wire a tiny bit. A twisting wire can show forces far too small for a spring.

items.p: Cavendish watched his experiment through a telescope from outside the room. Why do you think he did this?
items.a: So that he wouldn't disturb it. Even the warmth of his body could move the air and twist the wire. The force he was looking for was tiny.
items.why: When you look for something very small, you have to keep everything else still and the same.

items.p: Why did scientists stop using the metal cylinder in Paris, Le Grand K, to define the kilogram in 2019?
opts: It and its copies were slowly drifting apart by tiny amounts
It was too heavy to lift
items.why: Metal can slowly change. The copies and the original drifted apart by tiny amounts. So now the kilogram is fixed by the Planck constant, a constant of nature. As far as anyone can measure, it never changes.

items.p: The Indus Valley cities, about 4,500 years ago, had stone weights in sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. What comes next?
items.why: Each weight is double the one before. Double 32 is 64. Picking 33 usually means the pattern was taken as adding 1. Picking 48 means adding 16.

items.p: A forcemeter in a freely falling lift would read zero, even with a bag on its hook.
items.why: True. Everything falls together, so the bag doesn't pull on the spring. Einstein used ideas like this to think about gravity in a new way.

items.p: Your homemade forcemeter showed 3 newtons for a pencil box. A kitchen scale showed it was 180 grams. Is your forcemeter right? Explain.
items.a: Not quite. 180 grams pulls with about 1.8 newtons, which is nearly 2. My forcemeter showed 3, which is too big. Maybe my zero was wrong, or the band got stretched.
items.why: 100 grams pulls with about 1 newton, so divide the grams by 100. If the two don't match, check the zero and the marks.

items.p: A shop's hanging spring balance shows 1 kilogram with nothing on the hook. A customer buys what the balance says is 3 kilograms of onions. How many kilograms of onions do they really get?
items.why: The balance started at 1 instead of 0, so every reading is 1 kilogram too big. 3 take away 1 is 2 kilograms. That is why Legal Metrology officers check scales.

items.p: In the fair scale challenge, you used water to check a scale. Why is water a good standard to use?
items.a: One litre of water always has a mass of about 1 kilogram. Everybody can get water and fill a bottle with a jug. Nobody owns it.
items.why: The gram was first defined in 1795 using water. Water is a standard that nature gives everyone.

items.p: Which of these is the biggest force?
opts: The Saturn V rocket lifting off
The Earth and the Moon pulling on each other
items.why: The Earth and the Moon pull on each other with about 200 million million million newtons. The Saturn V pushed with about 34 million. Picking the rocket usually means things we can see seem bigger than the pull between worlds.

items.p: Isaac Newton said he did not know how gravity reaches across empty space. Einstein said gravity is bent space and time. Others think it might be carried by a particle called a graviton. Which idea do you find easiest to imagine? Why?
items.a: Any answer with a reason is good. For example: I like Einstein's idea, because I can imagine a ball rolling into a dip in a stretched sheet.
items.why: Scientists still don't agree on the deepest answer. That's an open question you could work on one day.

items.p: Put these steps for using a forcemeter in the right order: read at eye level, check the zero, write the number with its unit, hook on and pull steadily.
items: write the number with its unit
items.why: First check the zero, so the reading starts fair. Then pull, read and write it down.

items.p: The size-weight illusion means a big box always feels heavier than a small box of the same weight.
items.why: False. It is the other way round. The small box feels heavier, because we expect big things to be heavy.

items.p: Design a forcemeter that could show the pull of a single sheet of paper. Draw it and label how it works.
items.a: For example, a long plastic ruler taped to a table edge, sticking out. The paper hangs from the far end, and a straw pointer shows the bend.
items.why: A good design is sensitive: a small pull makes a big, easy-to-see movement.

items.p: Why do scientists say 'about 10 newtons' for a 1 kilogram bag, and not exactly 10?
opts: Because the exact number is about 9.8 newtons on Earth
Because nobody has ever measured it
items.why: On Earth, 1 kilogram pulls down with about 9.8 newtons. It even changes a tiny bit from place to place. 10 is close enough for most everyday sums.
