quiz.p: In the coin-pull test, what made 'one coin' a fair unit of pull?
opts: Every coin of one kind pulls by the same amount
Any mix of coins and buttons works just as well
quiz.why: A unit must be the same every time, and coins of one kind are. Picking 'any mix works' misses something. A button pulls less than a coin, so a count of mixed things means nothing.

quiz.p: In the coin-pull test, you needed 6 big coins to start a notebook sliding. A friend needed 12 small coins for the same notebook on the same table. Who found the bigger pull?
opts: Neither. It was the same pull, counted in different units
quiz.why: Same notebook, same table, same pull. Only the unit changed. Picking 'your friend' means trusting the number 12 without asking what it counts.

quiz.p: Why did people around the world agree to share one unit of force?
opts: So that everyone's numbers can be compared
Because forces are made of newtons
quiz.why: A shared unit lets a pull in Pune be compared with a pull in Paris. Picking 'made of newtons' mixes up the force with the unit we count it in. The newton is an agreement between people. Newton died in 1727, long before the unit got his name in 1948.

quiz.p: What is the unit of force?
quiz.why: The newton is the unit of force. The kilogram is a unit of mass. The forcemeter is the tool, not the unit.

quiz.p: About how hard does a small apple pull down on your hand?
quiz.why: A small apple of about 100 grams pulls with about 1 newton. Picking 100 usually means grams and newtons were mixed up.
The pointer is on the small mark between 6 and 7. Each small mark is half a newton. So the reading is 6 and a half newtons.

chart.title: A forcemeter. Each small mark is half a newton.

quiz.p: With nothing on the hook, a forcemeter's pointer is not on zero. What should you do?
opts: Turn the zero screw until the pointer is on zero
quiz.why: Set the pointer to zero first, or every reading will be wrong by the same amount.

quiz.p: What is inside a forcemeter that stretches when you pull?
quiz.why: A spring. The harder the pull, the further it stretches, and the further the pointer moves.

quiz.p: If you pull a forcemeter twice as hard, what happens to the spring?
opts: It stretches about twice as far
quiz.why: Twice the pull gives about twice the stretch, as long as you don't pull past the forcemeter's range. Robert Hooke published this in 1678.

quiz.p: In the coin-pull test, you did each test 3 times and used the middle number. Why?
opts: Because one try can be a fluke
quiz.why: A bump or a crooked notebook can spoil one try. The middle of three tries is less likely to be spoiled. That makes the test fair.

quiz.p: A 1 kilogram bag of rice pulls a forcemeter with about 10 newtons on Earth. About what would it show on the Moon?
quiz.why: The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard. Picking 10 usually means weight is thought never to change. Picking 60 means multiplying by 6 instead of dividing.

quiz.p: You stand on a bathroom scale and press down on a table beside you. The number goes down. Why?
opts: The table holds up part of you, so you push less on the scale
quiz.why: The scale shows your push, not how much of you there is. The table now shares the job of holding you up.

opts: It changes how a thing moves, or changes its shape
It is needed to keep anything moving
It is a kind of stuff inside heavy things
quiz.why: A force changes movement. Picking 'needed to keep anything moving' is Aristotle's old idea. Galileo and Newton showed that things slow down because friction pulls back, not because the push runs out.

quiz.p: You press your palm on a table. What is happening at the size of atoms?
opts: The electrons of your hand push the electrons of the table away
Your atoms flow into the table
quiz.why: Electrons push other electrons away, so your hand never quite touches the table. That push is what you feel. Picking 'atoms flow in' imagines atoms mixing. They push apart instead.

quiz.p: Do scientists all agree on what gravity really is?
opts: Yes, it was settled long ago
No. Newton, Einstein and particle physicists give different pictures, and it is still being studied
quiz.why: We can put very exact numbers on gravity's pull. What it is, deep down, is still an open question.

open_questions.q: What is a force, really, deep down?
open_questions.why_open: Newton could describe gravity but not explain it. Einstein said gravity is bent space and time. Particle physicists think forces are carried by particles. Nobody has joined these into one picture.

open_questions.q: Does a graviton, a particle that carries gravity, exist?
open_questions.why_open: Many physicists think it should. It would be so hard to catch that nobody knows how to build an experiment to find one.

open_questions.q: Why do measurements of gravity's strength disagree?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have measured the strength of gravity, often called big G, many times since Cavendish. The best results still disagree more than they should. Nobody is sure why.

open_questions.q: How small a force can we ever measure?
open_questions.why_open: Quantum physics says measuring always nudges things a little. Clever new tools can get around some limits. Nobody knows how far this can go.

open_questions.q: Exactly why does a small box feel heavier than a big box of the same weight?
open_questions.why_open: The size-weight illusion was described in 1891. Scientists still argue about how much comes from what we expect, and how much from how we grip and lift.

open_questions.q: How do millions of tiny molecular pulls work together to make a muscle strong and smooth?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can find one molecule's pull. How so many of them work together so well is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Is the strength of gravity the same everywhere in the universe, and at every time?
open_questions.why_open: As far as we can tell, yes. But scientists keep testing it. If it changed even a little, our ideas about the universe would have to change.

open_questions.q: Why does the pull needed to slide something grow so evenly with its weight?
open_questions.why_open: Leonardo da Vinci noticed this rule around 1500, and Guillaume Amontons wrote it down in 1699. It works well. But why it works, at the size of atoms, is still being studied. It seems to depend on how many tiny bumps really touch.

maths.problem: In the coin-pull investigation, Meera needed 6 five-rupee coins to start her notebook sliding. Her father tested the same notebook with one-rupee coins and needed 12. On a ruler balance, one five-rupee coin balanced two one-rupee coins. Did they find the same pull, or different pulls?
maths.answer: The same pull. 6 five-rupee coins pull as hard as 12 one-rupee coins.
maths.explain: One five-rupee coin pulls as hard as 2 one-rupee coins. So 6 five-rupee coins pull as hard as 6 lots of 2 one-rupee coins. 6 times 2 is 12. Meera's father needed 12. The numbers were different, but the pull was the same. Only the unit was different.
maths.why_maths: Two numbers can only be compared in the same unit. Multiplying turns one unit into the other, the way you change rupees into paise.
maths.context: In the coin-pull investigation, you dropped coins into a hanging cup until a notebook started to slide. These numbers are made up.

maths.problem: Here are made-up results from the coin-pull investigation. One notebook needed 6 coins. Two stacked notebooks needed 12. Three needed 17. Spot the pattern. About how many coins would four notebooks need? Why?
maths.answer: About 23 coins, because each extra notebook needs about 6 more coins.
maths.explain: From 1 notebook to 2, the coins went up by 6. From 2 to 3, they went up by 5. So each notebook adds about 5 or 6 coins. 17 add 6 is 23. Real results are never perfectly even, so 22, 23 or 24 are all good predictions. If you have a fourth notebook, test your prediction.

maths.problem: In the story Ten Packets of Salt, Mohan Lal's balance was set wrongly. Ten 1 kilogram packets of salt showed as only 5 kilograms. Basanti's basket showed 14 kilograms on the same balance. Something is odd. What was going wrong, and how heavy was the basket really?
maths.answer: The balance showed 5 kilograms too little every time. The basket was really 19 kilograms.
maths.explain: The ten packets were agreed to be 10 kilograms, but the balance said 5. So it was 5 kilograms short. Its pointer started in the wrong place, so every reading was short by the same 5. To fix a reading, add 5 back. 14 add 5 is 19. That is exactly what the balance showed once the zero was fixed.
maths.why_maths: When a scale's zero is wrong, every reading is out by the same amount. Finding that amount once, with something everyone agrees on, fixes every reading.
maths.context: In the story Ten Packets of Salt, Pushpa tested a spring balance with ten 1 kilogram packets. In the fair scale challenge, you checked a scale in the same way, with water.

maths.problem: In the forcemeter tug of war, Asha's forcemeter showed 5 newtons, and her father's showed 5 newtons too. Her father said, 'So together we are pulling with 10 newtons.' Is he right? Explain.
maths.answer: No. The pull through the two forcemeters is 5 newtons. Each forcemeter shows the same pull, seen from its own end.
maths.explain: Asha pulls on her father with 5 newtons, and he pulls back on her with 5 newtons. Both forcemeters feel that one pull passing through them. Adding 5 and 5 counts the same pull twice. If he let go, both forcemeters would drop to 0 together.
maths.why_maths: Adding only makes sense when the numbers count different things. Asking 'what does each number count?' stops you adding the same thing twice.
maths.context: In the forcemeter tug of war, two people hook two forcemeters together and pull. They read both forcemeters.

maths.problem: In the Moon tiffin activity, your 600 gram tiffin pulled with about 6 newtons on Earth. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard. Predict: about how hard would the same tiffin pull on the Moon?
maths.explain: One sixth means sharing into 6 equal parts and taking one part. 6 newtons shared into 6 parts is 1 newton each. So on the Moon the tiffin pulls with about 1 newton, like a small apple on Earth.
maths.why_maths: Sharing a force into equal parts shows how much weaker the Moon's pull is than the Earth's.
maths.context: In the Moon tiffin activity, you poured out rice to feel how light your lunch would be on the Moon.

maths.problem: In the pull detective experiment, these were the biggest readings. Slipper 2 newtons, drawer 5 newtons, cupboard door 6 newtons, chair 15 newtons, fridge door 18 newtons, school bag 25 newtons. Draw a bar chart. How much bigger is the fridge door's pull than the drawer's?
maths.answer: The fridge door's pull is 13 newtons bigger. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each pull, as tall as its reading. Then compare the fridge door and the drawer. 18 take away 5 is 13. So the fridge door needs 13 newtons more.
maths.why_maths: After the pull detective test you have six numbers. A bar chart shows the biggest and smallest pulls at a glance.

how_we_found_out.who: French scientists in 1795, and the countries that share the kilogram
how_we_found_out.story: For most of history, every town had its own weights. A ser in one market was not a ser in the next. So people often argued about how much they had bought. In 1795, France made a new rule. A gram would be the weight of a tiny cube of water, 1 centimetre on each side. Water is the same everywhere, so anyone could check it. In 1889, many countries agreed to share one kilogram. It was a metal cylinder, kept locked near Paris. Each country got a copy. India's copy is in New Delhi. People thought the metal would never change. But years later, the copies were weighed against it again. They no longer matched exactly. So in 2019, scientists stopped using the metal cylinder. Now the kilogram is set by a fixed number from physics. Anyone with the right machine can check it, anywhere in the world.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed one guarded lump of metal would stay exactly the same for ever. When the copies were checked years later, they had drifted apart by a tiny amount.

roots.context: We have been inventing units of pull, counting coins and water, and meeting the newton. Now we ask what a number like '5 newtons' really is, and what that says about us and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Nature has pushes and pulls, but it has no numbers. Numbers are a language people made together, so that everyone means the same thing. A newton is a word in that shared language.
deep_truth.habit: We think a number is part of a thing, like its colour. But the same pull on the notebook was 6 big coins or 12 small coins. The pull stayed the same. Only the words for it changed.
deep_truth.evidence: In the coin-pull test, two careful people got different numbers for the same notebook, and both were right. They were using different words for the same pull.

three.who_am_i: You can feel a pull, but you cannot give it a number on your own. Your number means something only when someone shares your unit.
three.what_is_life: A crow feels the wind and a root senses which way is down, with no numbers at all. People add numbers so they can share what they sense.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth pulled on mangoes long before anyone had a unit. The pull belongs to the world. The number belongs to the people who agreed on it.

roots.thread: Before any unit, there is only the pull itself, with no number on it. Then people choose one small pull and call it One: one coin, one ratti seed, one newton. From that One come all the numbers, from a molecule's tug to the pull between the Earth and the Moon. DeepKids sees in this a small picture of the One becoming the many. Every number is counted from one shared One, and it means something only because the One is shared.

teachings.teaching: Truth is one. The wise call it by many names.
teachings.link: One notebook's pull was called 6 big coins, 12 small coins and half a newton. The names changed with the unit. The pull itself stayed one.

teachings.teaching: The heavens were raised, and a balance was set. So do not cheat the balance. Weigh fairly, and do not make the balance short.
teachings.link: A balance is a promise between people. In the story Ten Packets of Salt, one wrong pointer cheated every porter, until a shared standard showed it.

science.text: Since 20 May 2019, the kilogram, and so the newton, is fixed by the Planck constant, a constant of nature. People still chose the exact number it is given, so the new kilogram matched the old one. A Kibble balance can turn that number into a real kilogram anywhere.
Every unit is chosen by people. Philosophers of science still argue about the laws of nature. Are they simply found, or partly shaped by how we choose to describe and count things?

other_view.who: Protagoras, a Greek thinker of about 2,400 years ago, as Plato reports in the Theaetetus
other_view.view: Protagoras said that each person is the measure of all things. What feels heavy to you is heavy for you. On this view, the feeling in your own hand is the truest measure. A shared unit only hides how differently each of us meets the world.
